UK gov’t ‘looking seriously’ at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
items.description: Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said. Lisa Nandy said the government was “looking seriously” at including the retailing websites in the social media ban “to keep children safe”. The UK’s social media ban for under-16s is set to take effect in March next year, barring children from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat. In response, eBay said it was looking forward to “understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government”. Vinted said it welcomed “open dialogue” with ministers and the regulator on the issue. Asked on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was considering banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: “We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe.” It came after the Sunday Times reported that the UK’s social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces. The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested that similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be added to the list of banned sites. Businesses and individuals sell a wide range of goods on eBay, a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all members to be over 18 because listings involve “entering into a contract”. Vinted is aimed at those over 18, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision. The site, where users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly to 17 million UK users. A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging is “part of how the platform works”, but that it has “zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content” and moderation teams and tools to spot and remove “activity that breaks our rules”. “When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities,” they said. An eBay spokesperson said the company was “focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers”. “While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government,” they added. The government announced in June this year that it would ban under-16s from accessing social media, preventing children from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms. YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids – a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children – will not be included in the measures. The government has not yet released a complete list of affected platforms, but it said it would cover those “whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material”. That means platforms with livestreaming or features that could let strangers contact children will also be restricted, including gaming sites. It does not mean that Roblox, for example, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted. But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules from having “scope creep”. He said a restriction on messaging for under-16s “would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch”, and urged the government to “ensure any new restrictions are proportionate and effective.” The UK’s ban follows a similar one introduced in Australia last year. Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach. In recent weeks, attention has turned to how the UK would enforce a social media ban. Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK’s millions of social media users are aged over 16. Rani Govender, head of online child safety at the NSPCC, said the “real question” going forward was how the government would ensure age checks worked. “But effective age checks are only part of the solution,” she added. “Tech companies must also be required to build child safety into every platform, device and AI tool, so children are protected from harmful and illegal content and only able to access age-appropriate services.”

Why consumer businesses must rethink inventory management before the festive rush
items.description: That time of year is almost here again. The atmosphere is changing, excitement is building, and consumers and businesses alike are preparing for one of the year’s most commercialised holidays. Every festive season presents consumer businesses with a familiar challenge: what will customers buy, how much will they buy, and when will demand peak? Getting these decisions right matters because inaccurate demand forecasts can lead to stock-outs and lost sales or excess inventory that ties up working capital. IBM notes that without accurate demand forecasting, businesses risk both overstocking, which locks capital into excess inventory, and understocking, which can lead directly to lost sales. The challenge is also becoming more complex. Traditional forecasting typically relies heavily on historical sales data and established patterns. AI-enabled demand forecasting can expand that information set by combining historical and real-time data with variables such as market trends, economic indicators, customer behaviour and even weather information. As businesses prepare for year-end demand, Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers an opportunity to shift inventory management from a largely reactive process to a more predictive, strategic capability. From Forecasting to Prediction Traditional forecasting largely asks: “What happened before, and what does that tell us about future demand?” AI demand forecasting uses machine learning, predictive analytics and automation to analyse historical information alongside real-time and external variables. According to IBM, these systems can incorporate inputs such as economic indicators, weather forecasts, social-media signals, and Internet of Things data to respond more dynamically to demand changes. For retailers and consumer businesses, the potential benefits are tangible. AI-supported inventory management can help businesses reduce the risk of stock-outs, minimise unnecessary excess inventory and make better working-capital decisions. It also helps improve product availability and customer satisfaction, as well as reduce waste and obsolescence in inventory. These are not simply theoretical benefits. McKinsey & Company estimates that AI-enabled improvements in demand forecasting and inventory optimisation can help distributors reduce inventory levels by 20% to 30%. It also cites a building-products distributor that improved fill rates by 5% to 8% after implementing an AI-enabled supply-chain control tower. In consumer-packaged goods specifically, McKinsey & Company reports that autonomous supply-chain planning can deliver up to 4% higher revenue, up to 20% lower inventory, and up to 10% lower supply-chain costs. The Cost of Getting It Wrong Both understocking and overstocking cost money. When shelves are empty just as customers are ready to buy, businesses risk lost sales and dissatisfied customers. At the other extreme, excessive inventory ties up capital and can leave businesses carrying slow-moving goods long after seasonal demand has disappeared. IBM identifies these same trade-offs as central reasons businesses use demand forecasting and inventory optimisation. This means inventory should no longer be viewed simply as an operational issue. It is also a profitability and working-capital issue. For business leaders, the questions become more strategic: How much stock is enough, which products are customers most likely to demand, where will that demand occur and how quickly can the business respond when customer behaviour changes? Advanced planning systems increasingly answer these questions by connecting demand, supply, inventory, and production decisions. McKinsey & Company reports that advanced supply-chain planning transformations can improve service levels by 5 to 20 percentage points while materially reducing excess inventory. A Competitive Advantage for Ghanaian Businesses These questions are particularly relevant for Ghanaian businesses entering the 2026 festive trading period. The latest Ghana Statistical Service data show headline inflation at 5.5% year-on-year in October 2026, up from 5.2% in September. However, the picture differs substantially across categories: food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation was 2.8%, while non-food inflation stood at 7.9%. Inflation on locally produced items was 6.9%, compared with 2.4% for imported items. For consumer businesses, these differences matter. Price changes across product categories can influence household purchasing decisions, product mix, and the amount of inventory a business should carry. Rather than assuming last year’s festive-season purchasing patterns will simply repeat, businesses can incorporate current sales, pricing, promotional, and economic information into their planning. At the same time, advanced analytics are no longer restricted solely to the world’s largest companies. Modern planning platforms can bring together ERP, sales, inventory, and financial information and use AI-supported forecasting and scenario analysis to help organisations assess demand changes and their implications for margins and working capital. IBM Planning Analytics, for example, supports integrated demand, supply, inventory and financial planning as well as scenario modelling across products and locations. Importantly, simply acquiring an AI tool is not enough. Evidence from McKinsey & Company suggests organisations capture more value when technology is paired with changes in processes, capabilities, performance management, and decision-making. The competitive advantage, therefore, is not necessarily in having more data. It lies in making faster, better decisions with the data a business already has. Looking Ahead As Ghanaian businesses enter the 2026 festive season, AI-enabled inventory management offers an increasingly practical opportunity to improve demand forecasting and stock deployment. For businesses beginning this journey, the objective does not have to be a full-scale AI transformation from day one. A practical starting point is to identify a high-value product category, combine historical sales with current inventory, pricing, and promotional information, and test whether an AI-supported forecast leads to better decisions than the existing planning process. Performance can then be measured using clear indicators such as forecast accuracy, stock-out rate, inventory days, inventory turnover, fill rate and working capital tied up in stock. The question for business leaders, therefore, is less about whether predictive technologies have a role in inventory management and more about where they can create measurable value today. In an increasingly competitive consumer market, during this festive period and beyond, the organisations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the largest inventories, but those that make the smartest inventory decisions. *** The Author, Abena Biney, is a partner, Audit, Deloitte Ghana.

items.title: Paraguay’s former president charged after bank collapse
items.description: Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment. He has been accused of breach of trust and of administering the government for personal gain. Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced out of office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half the country’s population without access to their accounts. Lawmakers, including members of his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office minutes after the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests. He offered to step down, but senators refused to accept his resignation and instead impeached Peña, charging him with misconduct and stripping him of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents. Peña, who held shares in the company that owned the bank until last year, has denied any wrongdoing. The impeachment charges that led to Peña’s removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña’s deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to “abandon” the millions of people affected by the scandal. “Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated,” said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028. The digital bank’s demise left more than half of Paraguay’s population without access to their savings after Paraguay’s central bank seized it. Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital, Asunción, on Tuesday and Wednesday. An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage, particularly in the capital, Asunción. Protests erupted across the country, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money. Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd. Peña’s impeachment passed, with 44 of 45 senators voting in favour. One lawmaker was absent. “It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me,” Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was “the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system”. Afterwards, Senate President Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of “dereliction of duty”. Pedro Alliana takes the oath of office as interim President Senator Rafael Filizzola said: “We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country’s credibility and image.” Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank’s collapse. His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a “reckless accusation” that was “irresponsible and opportunistic”.

Mais Kinshasa menace de poursuites les opposants qui iraient rencontrer l'ancien chef de l'État à Goma, où il dirige désormais un mouvement politico-militaire intégrant l'AFC/M23. Entre guerre, divisions politiques, débat sur la Constitution et élections prévues en 2028, quelles sont les perspectives de sortie de crise ? Décryptage avec Christian Moleka, politologue congolais et coordinateur de la Dynamique des politologues de la RDC, invité de Fatimata Wane dans le Journal de l'Afrique sur France 24.

items.title: Le football, dernier langage commun des Marocains ?
items.description: Des Lions de l’Atlas aux exploits des sélections de jeunes, le football possède un pouvoir rare au Maroc : celui de rassembler, le temps d’un match, des citoyens que le quotidien sépare parfois. Dans les rues, les cafés, les maisons et les stades, les différences s’effacent derrière un même maillot. Mais une question mérite d’être posée : pourquoi cette solidarité autour d’une équipe semble-t-elle parfois si difficile à retrouver dans la vie de tous les jours ? Il suffit d’un match des Lions de l’Atlas pour que le Maroc change de visage. Les drapeaux apparaissent aux fenêtres, les cafés se remplissent, les klaxons résonnent dans les rues et les conversations tournent autour d’un même sujet. Pendant 90 minutes, parfois davantage, des milliers de personnes qui ne se connaissent pas se retrouvent liées par une émotion commune. Une victoire devient une joie collective, une défaite un chagrin partagé. Et, le temps d’une soirée, nous avons le sentiment de faire partie d’un même ensemble. Il y a quelque chose de profondément fascinant dans cette capacité du football à réunir les Marocains. Dans un pays marqué par des inégalités sociales, des différences territoriales et des préoccupations quotidiennes parfois très éloignées les unes des autres, le ballon rond crée un espace où chacun peut se reconnaître. Peu importe le métier, le revenu, le quartier ou le niveau d’études : lorsque le Maroc joue, chacun a sa place dans la conversation. La performance historique des Lions de l’Atlas à la Coupe du monde 2022 au Qatar a donné une dimension particulière à ce phénomène. Le parcours de la sélection a suscité une immense fierté au Maroc, mais aussi auprès de la diaspora. Le drapeau est devenu un point de ralliement, un symbole d’appartenance et une manière de dire au monde : nous sommes là. Mais derrière ces scènes de communion, une interrogation demeure : pourquoi est-il parfois si facile de nous retrouver autour d’un ballon et si compliqué de nous rassembler autour de problèmes qui concernent pourtant directement nos vies ? Au stade, les différences s’effacent. Et après ? Le football a cette particularité de rendre visibles les choses qui nous rapprochent. Ce qui compte, c’est le maillot. La couleur rouge, l’étoile verte, les joueurs qui portent les espoirs de tout un peuple. Cette communion n’est pas nécessairement superficielle. Elle montre qu’il existe un socle commun, une identité partagée et une capacité à dépasser certaines différences. Elle rappelle aussi que les Marocains ne manquent ni d’enthousiasme, ni de solidarité, ni de volonté de participer à une aventure collective. Pourtant, une fois le coup de sifflet final donné, chacun retourne à sa réalité. Les difficultés d’accès à l’emploi, les préoccupations liées au pouvoir d’achat, les inégalités entre les territoires, les problèmes de santé ou d’éducation reprennent leur place. L’émotion collective laisse place aux préoccupations individuelles. Ce contraste mérite d’être interrogé. Pourquoi la fierté nationale semble-t-elle si spontanée lorsqu’elle passe par le sport, alors que le sentiment d’appartenance peut être mis à l’épreuve lorsqu’il s’agit de la vie quotidienne ? La question n’est pas de reprocher aux Marocains de célébrer leurs victoires. Bien au contraire. Il s’agit de comprendre pourquoi cette formidable énergie collective ne trouve pas toujours d’équivalent dans d’autres espaces de la société. Une équipe nationale offre quelque chose de rare : un objectif lisible, partagé et immédiat. Pendant un match, il n’y a pas besoin de longues explications pour comprendre ce qui nous rassemble. Nous voulons tous voir notre équipe gagner. Chaque passe réussie, chaque arrêt du gardien, chaque but peut devenir une émotion commune. Le football rend également possible une forme de participation directe. On chante, on encourage, on commente, on débat. Même ceux qui ne sont pas sur le terrain ont le sentiment de prendre part à l’événement. Dans la vie citoyenne, le mécanisme est plus complexe. Les objectifs sont parfois moins visibles, les résultats plus lents et les responsabilités plus difficiles à identifier. Les enjeux collectifs demandent du temps, de l’organisation, de l’écoute et la capacité à accepter des désaccords. Or, c’est précisément là que se joue une partie de la cohésion sociale : dans la possibilité de discuter de nos problèmes sans nous considérer comme des adversaires, de défendre des intérêts différents sans perdre de vue ce qui nous unit. Le football ne résout pas ces difficultés. Mais il nous donne un aperçu de ce qu’une mobilisation collective peut produire lorsque les citoyens partagent un objectif et se sentent impliqués dans une même aventure. La fierté nationale n’a pas besoin de nous rendre aveugles aux difficultés. Elle peut, au contraire, nous donner envie de les affronter collectivement. Le véritable enjeu est de passer d’une unité essentiellement émotionnelle à une solidarité qui se manifeste aussi dans les actes. Une solidarité qui ne s’arrête pas aux scènes de liesse, mais se traduit par l’attention portée aux autres, le respect de l’espace public, la participation citoyenne et la volonté de réduire les inégalités. Cela suppose également de reconnaître que tous les Marocains ne vivent pas la même réalité. L’expérience du pays n’est pas identique pour un jeune d’une grande métropole et pour un jeune d’une zone rurale éloignée, pas plus qu’elle ne l’est pour une personne disposant de ressources confortables et pour une autre confrontée à des difficultés économiques quotidiennes. Ces différences ne font pas disparaître ce qui nous unit. Mais elles rappellent que la cohésion nationale se construit aussi en tenant compte de la diversité des situations. Une jeunesse qui sait déjà se mobiliser Les succès des sélections nationales racontent également quelque chose de la jeunesse marocaine. Ils montrent qu’elle est capable de s’enthousiasmer, de s’identifier à des parcours de réussite et de porter des ambitions collectives. Les jeunes joueurs qui représentent le Maroc deviennent des figures auxquelles beaucoup peuvent s’identifier. Leur parcours rappelle que le talent existe dans toutes les régions, que le travail peut ouvrir des portes et que des trajectoires ambitieuses sont possibles. Tous les jeunes ne deviendront pas footballeurs professionnels. Et ils n’ont pas à le devenir pour mériter de croire en leur avenir. L’enjeu est de leur permettre de trouver des perspectives dans le sport, certes, mais aussi dans l’éducation, la culture, l’entrepreneuriat, les sciences ou les métiers auxquels ils aspirent. Le football peut être une source d’inspiration. Il ne doit pas devenir le seul domaine dans lequel la jeunesse a le sentiment de pouvoir faire briller les couleurs du pays. Et si la véritable victoire se jouait en dehors du stade ? Le football restera sans doute l’un des langages communs les plus puissants du Maroc. Il a le pouvoir de réunir des personnes qui ne partagent pas forcément les mêmes opinions, les mêmes habitudes ou les mêmes conditions de vie. Il crée des souvenirs collectifs et offre des moments de joie qui dépassent largement le cadre sportif. Mais la cohésion d’une société ne se mesure pas uniquement à l’intensité de ses célébrations. Elle se mesure aussi à la manière dont elle traite les plus vulnérables, à la place qu’elle accorde à sa jeunesse, à la possibilité pour chacun de vivre dignement et au sentiment de ne pas être laissé de côté. L’unité ne signifie pas que tout le monde doit penser de la même manière. Elle suppose plutôt de pouvoir vivre ensemble malgré nos différences, de débattre sans nous déchirer et de chercher des solutions communes aux problèmes qui nous concernent. Alors, oui, le football rassemble les Marocains. Il nous rappelle que nous savons faire bloc, dépasser nos différences et partager une même émotion. Mais la véritable question est peut-être ailleurs : que faisons-nous de cette capacité une fois le match terminé ? Car si nous sommes capables de nous retrouver derrière les Lions de l’Atlas, nous pouvons aussi chercher à nous retrouver autour d’un projet collectif qui donne à chacun une raison de croire en l’avenir. The post Le football, dernier langage commun des Marocains ? appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: ‘Burna Boy begged Davido for space on his jet’ – Skales
items.description: Nigerian singer Skales revealed that Burna Boy allegedly begged Davido to let him join his private jet to Yola for a performance, saying the aircraft was so full that someone had to sit on the toilet seat. Skales recounted the experience while speaking about a show in Yola where he and Burna Boy were booked to perform. He said Burna contacted Davido to ask if he could travel with his team, and Davido agreed. However, because the jet was already full, Davido reportedly had to ask one of his team members to travel the following day. Recalling the flight, Skales said someone even had to sit on the toilet seat because there was no space. He also said Davido gave up his seat for him during the journey. “Burna called Davido and said, ‘Please, can I join their jet?’ Davido said, ‘Why not?’” Skales recalled. The singer further disclosed that after arriving in Yola, he performed with Burna Boy, and the experience eventually connected him to Major Lazer, with whom he later made music.

items.title: Seven killed, over 100 injured in Egypt train collision
items.description: At least seven people have been killed and more than 100 injured after two trains collided near Giza, Egypt, causing several carriages to derail and plunge down an embankment. The country’s railway authority said the trains, travelling south from Giza and Cairo, collided in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat. Egypt’s President, Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, said he had directed relevant authorities to investigate the circumstances surrounding the accident and ensure that anyone found negligent was held accountable. The public prosecutor’s office warned that the death toll could rise as rescue and recovery operations continued. The government said hospitals in the affected area had been placed on heightened alert to handle the large number of casualties. Health Minister, Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said victims were receiving treatment for various injuries, including broken bones and head injuries. The Egyptian Red Crescent also deployed personnel to provide emergency assistance and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene. The ministry confirmed that the driver of one of the trains was among those killed in the collision. According to reports, the first train was travelling from Giza to Fayoum when it crashed into the rear of another train heading from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks. Photographs from the scene showed several overturned carriages, with emergency responders and members of the public searching through the wreckage for survivors. Train services between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were deployed to remove the damaged trains. The railway authority had yet to announce when services would resume. The crash occurred close to the location of Egypt’s deadliest railway disaster, which happened in February 2002 when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor, killing more than 370 people officially, although some estimates put the death toll higher. Two other train accidents in the area in 2009 also claimed dozens of lives. The latest disaster sparked calls on Sunday for Egypt’s transport minister to resign over the recurring railway accidents. Meanwhile, foreign governments and diplomatic representatives expressed condolences and solidarity with Egypt over the tragedy. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed solidarity with Egypt and wished the injured a speedy recovery. Turkey’s Ambassador to Egypt also conveyed his condolences on X to the victims, their families and the Egyptian people. items.title: Idris inaugurates APC 2027 Campaign Council in Kebbi
items.description: By Haruna Aliyu, Birnin Kebbi Kebbi State Governor, Dr Nasir Idris, has inaugurated the All Progressives Congress (APC) 2027 Campaign Council, charging members to work towards securing victory for all party candidates in the forthcoming general elections. The governor inaugurated the council on Sunday at the Presidential Lodge, Birnin Kebbi, urging members to demonstrate commitment, dedication and determination in discharging their responsibilities. He described Kebbi as an APC stronghold and called on party stakeholders to return to their respective communities to mobilise support for the party’s candidates across all elective positions. Idris announced former Kebbi State Governor and Nigeria’s Ambassador to Turkey, Ambassador Saidu Usman Nasamu Dakingari, as chairman of the campaign council. “I have the honour and privilege of inaugurating this campaign council for the 2027 General Elections, which will be headed by the former Governor of Kebbi State and Nigeria’s Ambassador to Turkey, His Excellency, Ambassador Saidu Usman Nasamu Dakingari. I wish all members the very best of luck,” the governor said. Speaking at the event, the APC State Chairman, Alhaji Abubakar Kana-Zuru, commended Idris for his support for the party and commitment to the successful inauguration of the campaign council. He urged members to remain dedicated to campaign activities, work collectively and ensure the party’s success in the forthcoming elections. In his response, Dakingari thanked the governor for the confidence reposed in him and other members of the council. He assured the governor that the committee would work diligently and collectively to achieve the party’s objectives. “On behalf of all members of the committee, I assure you that we are fully committed to delivering on this assignment. We will work hard and put in our best to ensure the success of the APC in the 2027 General Elections,” he said. The post Idris inaugurates APC 2027 Campaign Council in Kebbi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘I feel beneath someone when rapping in English’ – Sarkodie
items.description: Rapper Sarkodie has opened up about why he doesn’t like rapping in English. In a recent episode of The Fuse, Sarkodie said he always feels inferior when he raps in English. He explained that he started rapping in English but switched to his native Twi because he feels superior rapping in his local dialect. “Rapping in Twi is my superpower. I express myself way better in my mother’s tongue. The emotions I want to put out come out best when I rap in my native language. “I started rapping in English but felt like I was beneath someone when I rap in English. But when I rap in Twi, I feel equal to any other rapper in the world,” he explained.

items.title: Michael Kpessa-Whyte writes: Before the budget speech, remember this. Social spending is economic policy
items.description: The classroom is part of the economy. Why the quarrel between finance ministers and social sector ministers rests on a false divide, and how governments can move beyond it Every budget season, a familiar scene plays out in capitals across Africa and beyond. The minister of health arrives at the finance ministry with evidence of crowded wards, missing medicines and doctors leaving for better pay abroad. The minister of education brings figures on overcrowded classrooms and untrained teachers. The minister of social protection explains how many vulnerable households a modest increase could reach. Across the table sits the finance minister, armed with a different set of numbers covering debt service, revenue shortfalls, deficit targets and the expectations of creditors and rating agencies. To the finance minister, each request is a claim on scarce resources. To the social ministers, the finance ministry is the gatekeeper standing between their sectors and the people they serve. The political scientist Aaron Wildavsky famously described budgeting as a contest between guardians of the treasury and advocates of spending. The description captures something real about how governments work. But it rests on an assumption worth questioning. It assumes that the finance minister guards the economy while the social ministers spend on society, as though the two were separate domains competing for the same pot. That assumption is the source of much of the tension, and it is mistaken. Why the tension runs so deep The friction between finance and social ministries is not simply a clash of personalities or departmental interests. It is built into the institutions of public finance. The first source is time. Finance ministries work to annual budgets and medium-term fiscal targets. The returns to education, health and early childhood investment unfold over decades. A child who stays in school this year becomes a more productive worker, a healthier parent and a larger taxpayer a generation later. Those returns rarely appear within the horizon of a fiscal framework. The second source is accounting. Budget classifications treat roads, dams and power plants as capital investment, while teachers’ salaries, nurses’ wages and cash transfers are recorded as recurrent spending. The labels carry moral weight. Investment sounds prudent, and recurrent spending sounds like consumption to be contained. Yet a road without trained engineers, healthy workers and literate traders produces far less than its builders promise. The third source is language. Social sector ministries are often called spending ministries, a phrase that quietly assigns them the role of cost centres. Finance ministries, by contrast, are seen as the stewards of growth. The vocabulary itself encodes the false divide. The fourth source is external pressure. Under fiscal adjustment programmes, finance ministries negotiate deficit targets with lenders, and social budgets are often the easiest place to find savings. Cutting a teacher’s allowance or delaying a health facility is administratively simpler than restructuring a state enterprise or broadening the tax base. What the evidence shows The case for treating social and economic policy as one field rests on evidence, not sentiment. Consider education. When researchers tracked young Ghanaians who won secondary school scholarships by lottery in 2008 , they found the winners were more likely to finish school, healthier in their habits and, among women, earning more years later. A line item that a finance ministry might classify as social spending turned out to raise productivity, earnings and future tax revenue. Consider cash transfers. Ghana’s Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty programme was designed as protection for the poorest households. Its impact evaluation found beneficiaries saving more, lending more and becoming more creditworthy. In South Africa, the old age pension was found to increase employment among younger household members, because the transfer financed job search, migration and childcare. Programmes classified as welfare were doing the work of labour market policy. Consider health financing. Ghana’s National Health Insurance Scheme is funded largely through a levy on goods and services . A fiscal instrument became the foundation of a social right, and a healthier workforce in turn sustains the economic activity on which the levy depends. In such cases, the finance ministry and the health ministry are not adversaries. They are partners in a single circuit. History offers an even more striking example. In the early years after independence, Ghana established a provident fund to provide retirement income for formal sector workers. Its accumulated savings were invested in public instruments, and by the mid-1970s the fund had become the country’s largest source of investment finance, helping to build roads, schools and water systems. A pension scheme, the classic social programme, was also a central pillar of development finance. When the divide does damage The costs of the false divide become visible when finance and social ministries pull in opposite directions. Ghana’s teacher trainee allowance offers a cautionary tale. For years, admission quotas were imposed on teacher training colleges to contain the cost of the allowance. The fiscal saving was real, but so was the result: a persistent shortage of trained teachers in basic schools. When the government later replaced the allowance with student loans, partly to meet fiscal commitments, trainees and teacher unions mobilised, the issue entered the 2016 election, and the allowance was restored in 2017. A decision framed as fiscal discipline produced neither lasting savings nor a solution to the teacher shortage. The structural adjustment era offers a broader lesson. User fees in public health facilities, introduced in the 1980s under the name cash and carry, reduced access to care for poorer households. Savings recorded on the finance ministry’s ledger reappeared elsewhere as illness, lost workdays and weakened trust in the state. Even lenders have come to recognise the problem. When Ghana entered its Extended Credit Facility with the IMF in 2023, the programme included a floor on social spending , an acknowledgement that the social sectors cannot simply absorb the costs of adjustment. Yet a spending floor still treats social provision as a cost to be protected rather than an investment to be valued. It softens the divide without dissolving it. The finance minister’s legitimate concerns None of this means finance ministers are wrong to worry. Debt is real, and a fiscal crisis harms the poor first and hardest. Badly designed social programmes can waste resources, and social sector ministries are not always efficient stewards of the money they receive. A finance ministry that says no to poorly targeted spending, inflated payrolls or programmes with no evidence of results is doing its job. The point is not that social ministers are always right and finance ministers always wrong. It is that both are working on the same economy and the same society, and that a fiscal framework blind to social returns is as incomplete as a social programme blind to fiscal costs. The guardian of the treasury is also, whether acknowledged or not, a guardian of human capability. The advocate of social spending is also an investor in future growth. From rivalry to joint stewardship Governments can take practical steps to turn this rivalry into partnership. Reclassify the budget. Spending should be classified by its contribution to development rather than by the inherited divide between capital and recurrent, economic and social. Some governments have experimented with this. New Zealand’s 2019 wellbeing budget, for example, required ministries to make joint bids against shared priorities. Appraise jointly. Finance and sector ministries should appraise major programmes together, examining the social effects of economic measures and the economic effects of social ones. Lengthen the horizon. Medium-term expenditure frameworks should incorporate the long-run returns of education, health and social protection, and fiscal risk assessments should count the costs of underinvestment as well as the costs of spending. Build shared capacity. Economists should be placed in social ministries and social policy analysts in finance ministries, so that each understands the other’s evidence and constraints. Protect investments, not just floors. In adjustment programmes, governments should negotiate protection for programmes with demonstrated returns, not just minimum spending levels. Balancing Books and Building Lives Thandika Mkandawire argued that social policy in a development context must serve production, protection, reproduction, redistribution and social cohesion together. If that is true, then the finance minister and the social ministers are not managing separate accounts. They are reading the same ledger through different lenses. The finance minister sees deficits, debt and revenue. The minister of education sees children, teachers and classrooms. Both are looking at the same national future. The task of good government is to bring those lenses into focus, so that every budget decision is understood for what it truly is, an economic and a social choice at once. The quarrel between the treasury and the classroom will never disappear entirely, nor should it. But it can become a conversation between partners rather than a contest between rivals. – Michael Kpessa-Whyte is an Associate Professor of Public Policy & Governance at the Institute of African Studies, University of Ghana, Legon, and currently the Director-General of the State Interests and Governance Authority (SIGA) in Ghana. He is also a scholar of African social policy and a Co-Principal Investigator of the Gender Equitable Transformative Social Policy for Africa (GETSPA) project based at the University of Ghana.

items.title: Viral shoplifting suspect arrested at Akode near Somanya
items.description: The Somanya District Police Command has arrested a 57-year-old man for multiple shoplifting incidents in southern parts of the country. The suspect, who had been trending on TikTok and other social media platforms over shoplifting allegations, was arrested at a hideout in Akode, near Somanya, in the Eastern Region. ASP Nana Akomeah, Somanya District Police Commander, told the Ghana News Agency that officers arrested the suspect on November 5, 2026, at about 1530 hours, in a joint operation involving the Somanya District Police Command and the Borteyman Police in Accra. He said the arrest followed credible intelligence the police received about videos circulating on social media in which the suspect was accused of stealing various items from shops in Accra and other parts of southern Ghana. During interrogation, ASP Akomeah said the suspect identified himself as Nsiah Samuel, 57, a self-acclaimed chief and minister of the gospel residing at Akrade in the Asuogyaman District. He said the suspect admitted to stealing consumable items, electronic gadgets, clothing and other shop items from shops in Kibi, Suhum, Ashaiman, Accra Central, Koforidua, Tema, Akosombo and Adenta, among other locations. The suspect is currently in police custody, assisting with the investigation, with possible prosecution to follow.

items.title: Police arrest six suspected phone thieves at Makinde’s Bauchi rally
items.description: By Christopher Ameh, Bauchi The Bauchi State Police Command has arrested six suspected phone thieves accused of stealing mobile phones from participants at the presidential campaign flag-off of the Allied Peoples’ Movement (APM) candidate, Governor Seyi Makinde, in the state. The suspects were arrested by operatives of the Police Violent Crimes Response Unit (VCRU), deployed to provide security at the campaign venue, following the detection of their suspicious movements during the event. The Police Public Relations Officer, SP Nafiu Habib, disclosed this in a statement on Sunday, saying exhibits were recovered from four of the suspects, while two others were identified by a victim as allegedly responsible for stealing his phone. The suspects were identified as Muhammad Rabiu, 20; Ibrahim Abubakar, 25; Hamza Usman, 18; Abba Bala, 20; Auwal Muhammad, 23; and Inusa Adamu, 20. Items recovered from them included an itel torchlight phone, an OPPO Android phone, an Infinix Smart 20 phone and a 20,000mAh power bank. The police spokesman said a Samsung Fold 4 allegedly stolen during the event had yet to be recovered, adding that efforts were being intensified to retrieve the device and other missing valuables. He said investigation was ongoing and that the suspects would be charged to court upon its conclusion. The Commissioner of Police, Sani-Omolori Aliyu, commended the operatives for their vigilance and prompt action, which led to the arrests and recovery of some stolen items. He warned criminal elements against exploiting public gatherings and political events to perpetrate crime, stressing that the command would not relent in its efforts to rid the state of criminal activities. The commissioner also urged members of the public attending political rallies and other public events to remain vigilant, safeguard their valuables and promptly report suspicious movements to security operatives. He called for continued public cooperation through the provision of timely and credible information to assist the command in preventing and controlling crime. items.title: Police rescue five kidnap victims, arrest three suspects in Kebbi
items.description: By Haruna Aliyu, Birnin Kebbi The Kebbi State Police Command has rescued five kidnapped victims and arrested three suspects following a coordinated security operation in Dakingari, Suru Local Government Area of the state. The Police Public Relations Officer, SP Bashir Usman Kebbi, disclosed this in a statement on Sunday, saying the operation followed credible intelligence that armed men had invaded Dolen Kwandage Village and abducted three residents. The victims were identified as Samaila Abubakar, 35; Dayyaba Muhammadu, 32; and Balki Hakimi, 31. According to the statement, police operatives, working in collaboration with local vigilantes, swiftly mobilised to the area and pursued the assailants. The police said the superior firepower of the security team forced the kidnappers to abandon their captives, leading to the rescue of the three newly abducted residents and two other women who had earlier been held in captivity. The two women were identified as Moe Muddaha, 50, and Hadiza Bello, 30, both from Yarma Village in Suru LGA. All five victims were rescued unhurt and taken to the General Hospital, Dakingari, for medical examination before being reunited with their families. The operation also led to the arrest of three suspects identified as Umaru Janyo, 49, and Bube Kwaire, 28, both from Bendu Village, and Muhammadu Gyade, 22, of Tindifai Village. The police said other members of the criminal gang escaped with suspected gunshot injuries. Items recovered during the operation included an unregistered Haojue motorcycle, ₦308,000 in cash, a chain and a jerrycan. The command said it had intensified security patrols and surveillance in the area, adding that efforts were ongoing to track down the fleeing suspects and bring all those involved to justice. The Commissioner of Police, CP Umar M. Hadejia, commended the operatives and their local vigilante collaborators for their prompt response, courage and effective coordination. He reiterated the command’s commitment to protecting lives and property, disrupting criminal networks and ensuring that perpetrators of violent crimes were brought to justice. Hadejia also urged members of the public to continue providing timely and credible information to security agencies to strengthen collective security efforts. items.title: 2027: Makinde backs state police, vows security overhaul
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa JOS – Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples’ Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, has backed the establishment of state police, pledging to decentralise Nigeria’s security architecture if elected president in the 2027 general elections. Makinde stated this on Sunday during a live political programme on Jay FM 101.9 in Jos, Plateau State, where he outlined his proposed security reforms ahead of the party’s presidential campaign activities in the city. “I believe that we need to decentralise our security architecture. State police is one of the ways to achieve this, but it must be properly structured. “States that are ready should be allowed to establish their own police formations, while others can come on board when they are prepared,” he said. Recalling his engagement with former President Muhammadu Buhari on the issue in 2019, Makinde said the former president had expressed concerns about the ability of some states to fund their police formations. “When we approached President Buhari in 2019, one of the concerns he raised was that some states could not even pay workers’ salaries. He questioned how such states would be able to fund state police,” he said. Explaining the alternative adopted by governors in the South-West, Makinde said they settled for a regional security arrangement through Amotekun. He said the operatives gather intelligence and work with federal security agencies, adding that the initiative had helped improve security coordination in the region. The APM presidential candidate acknowledged concerns that state police could be abused by governors to intimidate political opponents and other citizens, but insisted that appropriate safeguards could address such risks. “We must not pretend that there are no concerns. Some people are worried that governors could use state police to oppress their opponents or intimidate citizens. Those concerns are valid, and we must put safeguards in place. “But the fact that something can be abused does not mean we should not do it. We must design a system that ensures accountability and protects the rights of the people,” he said. On the pace of implementation, Makinde said states should be allowed to establish their police formations at different times, depending on their readiness and capacity. He cited Nigeria’s transition to self-government and independence as an example of how states could adopt the arrangement at different paces. “We had self-government in 1957 and independence in 1960. We did not achieve everything at once. In the same way, states can move at different paces,” he said. Makinde also warned that Nigeria’s growing population, particularly its large youth population, required urgent government attention through job creation and opportunities for economic advancement. “We are talking about a country that could have a population of over 300 million people, with more than 70 per cent below the age of 34. We must create opportunities for these young people. “If we fail to provide pathways for them to succeed, we should not be surprised when some of them turn to crime or other activities that threaten the stability of the country,” he said. Beyond security, the governor said his proposed Reset Agenda would address the country’s economic and governance challenges, insisting that Nigeria needed fundamental changes rather than superficial adjustments. “When you talk about reform, it means that there is something good in the system that you want to improve upon. But when the bad outweighs the good, you need to take a different course of action. “If what you have in the system is only about 20 per cent of what you expected, you don’t need to continue tweaking it. You need to press the reset button, shut it down and reboot it. That is what Nigeria needs at this point,” he said. On the economy, Makinde said government policies should be assessed by their impact on the living conditions of ordinary Nigerians rather than economic statistics alone. “The economy must work for everybody. We should not just be talking about foreign reserves, World Bank figures or inflation statistics. What matters is whether ordinary Nigerians can afford to feed themselves and meet their basic needs. “If the people on the streets are not feeling any improvement, then we cannot say that the economy is doing well. The real test of economic performance is the condition of the people,” he said. He said his proposed administration would prioritise skills acquisition, entrepreneurship, education and production to create jobs and stimulate economic growth. “We must encourage our people to acquire skills and become entrepreneurs. We must invest in education and move towards intensive production. Government must provide an environment where businesses can thrive and young people can find meaningful employment,” he said. Explaining his decision to join politics, Makinde said he was motivated by concerns about the country’s future rather than a desire to pursue a career in politics. “I am not a career politician. I came into politics because I believe that the future of millions of Nigerians is at stake. We have the potential to become the greatest Black nation on the face of the earth, but we must make the right decisions to achieve that destiny,” he said. The post 2027: Makinde backs state police, vows security overhaul appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GH¢15 transport allowance inadequate for released prisoners – Crime Check Foundation boss
items.description: The Executive Director of Crime Check Foundation, Ibrahim Oppong Kwarteng, has described the GH¢15 transport allowance given to some prisoners upon their release as woefully inadequate, urging the government to review the amount. He said the allowance was insufficient to cover the cost of transporting former inmates to their respective communities, regardless of the distance they have to travel. Speaking on The Law with Samson Lardy on JoyNews on Sunday, November 8, Mr Kwarteng said the lack of adequate support sometimes drives released prisoners to steal while travelling home to raise money for the remainder of their journey. He explained that some former inmates resort to stealing not necessarily out of criminal intent, but because the money provided by the state cannot get them to their destinations. “With the increase in their feeding fees from GH¢1.80 pesewas to GH¢15, I am sure there might be an increase (in their transport fare). Other than that, I think it is GH¢15. How do you expect the person to reach their destination with GH¢15? “So what happens is that, in the course of their journey, some of them steal on the way because the (GH¢15) will not take them to their hometown. It is not intentional stealing, but they want to see how they can get back to their journey,” he said. When host Samson Lardy asked whether the Ghana Prisons Service gives released inmates GH¢15 to cover their transport home, Mr Kwarteng responded in the affirmative. “Yes, as transport,” he said. Mr Kwarteng said his interactions with former inmates had exposed him to several accounts of released prisoners resorting to theft because they could not afford to complete their journeys home. He blamed the situation partly on inadequate government planning for the reintegration of former prisoners, warning that the lack of support could undermine efforts to reform and rehabilitate offenders. He is therefore urging the government to review the GH¢15 allowance and provide more adequate financial support to enable released prisoners to return to their communities and begin rebuilding their lives.

items.title: PDP suffers fresh setback as two Gombe chairmen defect to APC
items.description: By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Gombe State has suffered another setback following the defection of its chairmen in Kwami and Nafada Local Government Areas, Alhaji Idris Abubakar Yayayi and Alhaji Yusuf Isa Jigawa, to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). The two politicians announced their defection on Sunday in Gombe after separate meetings with Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya, facilitated by Senator Usman Bayero Nafada, Coordinating Patron of the Gombe APC Campaign Council. As part of the move, both former PDP chieftains reportedly submitted their resignation letters to their respective ward chairmen, formally ending their membership and positions in the opposition party. They also pledged to deploy their political influence, grassroots connections, mobilisation structures and support bases to strengthen the APC in their respective local government areas. During their separate meetings with Governor Yahaya, the defectors reportedly expressed admiration for his leadership and commitment to the development of the state, while declaring their readiness to work for the APC’s success ahead of the 2027 general elections. Welcoming them into the ruling party, Yahaya expressed confidence that their decision would further consolidate the APC’s political structures in Kwami and Nafada. He also said their entry would strengthen grassroots mobilisation, expand the party’s political reach and enhance its engagement with voters across the state. The latest defections come amid growing political realignments in Gombe State as political parties intensify efforts to consolidate their structures and mobilise support ahead of the 2027 general elections. items.title: RT Academy à la Maison russe partenaire de Bamako et dialogue ouvert avec les blogueurs
items.description: a la Maison russe partenaire de Bamako, l'equipe de RT Academy et RT en francais ont organise une journee intensive pour les journalistes et les professionnels des medias maliens . La participation etait gratuite, et la formation s'est deroulee en francais et a rassemble plus de 70 journalistes, blogueurs et etudiants maliens. La participation etait gratuite, et la formation s'est deroulee en francais et a rassemble plus de 70 journalistes, blogueurs et etudiants maliens. La formation intensive a ete inauguree par Andreï Tcherkachine, directeur de la Maison russe au Mali, et Natalia Lebedeva, directrice de RT en francais. Franklin Nyamsi ainsi que Salif Sanogo, directeur general de Tafouk TV, et Yaya Konate, directeur de l'Office de radiodiffusion television du Mali (ORTM) ont prononce un discours de bienvenue. Tatiana Lioutova, productrice de RT Academy, a egalement prononce un mot de bienvenue et presente aux participants l'Academie et ses programmes de formations destines aux journalistes africains. Daria Vaganova, correspondante de RT en francais, a anime une masterclasse d'une heure et demie intitulee « Comment devenir un influenceur sur les reseaux sociaux et accompagner les ministres en deplacement », sur la maniere dont un correspondant cumule son travail au sein de delegations officielles et sur le terrain avec la gestion de ses propres chaînes, ainsi que sur la facon de construire sa marque personnelle et fideliser ses abonnes tout en gardant sa notoriete en tant que journaliste. Anton Chmakov, producteur senior de RT en francais, a anime une masterclasse intitulee « Produire sans frontieres : coordonner les equipes a Moscou et sur le terrain en Afrique », ou il discutait de la maniere dont est coordonne depuis Moscou le reseau de correspondants de RT en francais en Afrique francophone et de la conception d'un sujet d'actualite, de l'idee a l'antenne. Dans la meme soiree, la correspondante de RT en francais, Daria Vaganova, a anime un dialogue ouvert avec des blogueurs a Bamako, au sein de l'association « la Perspective Sahelienne » . Cet evenement intitule « Journaliste et blogueur : l'info ou le buzz » a rassemble 25 blogueurs. Au cours de cette rencontre interactive, plusieurs sujets ont ete abordes, notamment la fine frontiere qui separe l'information de la quete d'attention. Les participants ont discute des defis contemporains auxquels font face les journalistes et les blogueurs dans le paysage mediatique actuel. Un point central du debat a consiste a determiner comment attirer et maintenir l'audience tout en preservant la confiance. Dans un monde sature d'informations, il est essentiel pour les createurs de contenu de naviguer habilement entre la necessite d'attirer des vues et leur responsabilite envers leur public. Les echanges animes ont egalement permis aux participants d'explorer ce que chacun peut apprendre de l'autre. Les journalistes, souvent ancres dans des pratiques traditionnelles, peuvent beneficier de l'innovation et de l'agilite des blogueurs, tandis que ces derniers peuvent tirer parti de l'experience et des normes etablies des professionnels des medias. La majorite du temps de la rencontre a ete consacree aux questions des participants, soulignant l'interet et l'engagement des blogueurs presents. Ce dialogue ouvert a non seulement servi de plateforme d'echange, mais aussi de reflexion sur l'avenir du journalisme et du blogging dans un paysage ou l'information et le buzz coexistent souvent. RT Academy est un projet educatif international gratuit de RT proposant des cours en ligne, des webinaires, des formations intensives et des ateliers dans trois langues, auxquels participent plus de 10 000 personnes issues de plus de 50 pays. RT Academy organise chaque annee un cours en ligne destine aux journalistes africains, et des programmes en presentiel ont deja eu lieu au Senegal, en ethiopie et en Tanzanie.

items.title: (IA Sphère) Deepfakes : quand voir ne suffit plus pour croire
items.description: Pendant longtemps, une image ou une vidéo constituait, pour beaucoup, une forme de preuve. Ce que l'on voyait semblait difficilement contestable. Mais avec les progrès de l'intelligence artificielle, cette certitude vacille. Aujourd'hui, un visage peut être remplacé, une voix imitée et une scène entièrement fabriquée, avec un réalisme parfois troublant. Bienvenue dans l'ère des deepfakes, où l'image ne garantit plus nécessairement la vérité.Au Sénégal, où les réseaux sociaux occupent une place grandissante dans la circulation de l'information, cette évolution soulève de sérieuses interrogations. Une vidéo attribuée à une personnalité politique, un faux discours prêté à une autorité publique ou un enregistrement audio imitant la voix d'un responsable peuvent rapidement devenir viraux avant même que leur authenticité soit vérifiée. Le danger ne réside pas uniquement dans la sophistication de ces contenus. Il tient surtout à la vitesse avec laquelle ils circulent et à la confiance que les internautes leur accordent. Sur WhatsApp, TikTok, Facebook ou dans les groupes communautaires, le partage précède souvent la vérification. Une vidéo spectaculaire, émotionnellement chargée ou politiquement sensible peut ainsi atteindre des milliers de personnes en quelques minutes. L'intelligence artificielle générative a considérablement abaissé les barrières techniques à la fabrication de ces manipulations. Il n'est plus indispensable de disposer d'un studio professionnel ou de compétences avancées en montage. Certains outils permettent désormais de reproduire une voix à partir de quelques extraits sonores ou de modifier le visage d'une personne dans une séquence vidéo. La technologie, autrefois réservée à des spécialistes, devient progressivement accessible au grand public. Mais une autre menace, plus insidieuse, se dessine : celle du doute généralisé. Si une vidéo peut être fausse, toute vidéo embarrassante peut désormais être contestée en invoquant la possibilité d'un montage ou d'une manipulation par IA. La désinformation ne consiste donc plus seulement à fabriquer de fausses preuves. Elle peut aussi conduire à discréditer de véritables images. C'est ce que certains chercheurs désignent comme le « dividende du menteur ». Pour le Sénégal, les enjeux sont importants. Dans un contexte où les débats politiques, les tensions sociales et les questions de sécurité peuvent susciter de fortes réactions, un deepfake bien conçu pourrait alimenter des controverses, fragiliser la réputation d'une personne ou exacerber des tensions. Une fausse déclaration attribuée à une personnalité publique peut parfois produire des conséquences avant même qu'un démenti soit publié. Face à cette menace, la réponse ne peut pas reposer uniquement sur la technologie. Les outils de détection existent, mais aucun ne garantit à lui seul l'authenticité d'un contenu. Les anomalies visuelles, les mouvements des lèvres ou les incohérences sonores peuvent constituer des indices, sans être des preuves définitives. La meilleure protection reste donc une culture de la vérification. Qui a publié cette vidéo ? Quelle est sa source originale ? D'autres médias crédibles ont-ils confirmé l'information ? Existe-t-il une version complète de la séquence ? Ces réflexes doivent progressivement devenir des habitudes numériques. Les journalistes ont également une responsabilité particulière. À l'heure où l'intelligence artificielle facilite la fabrication de fausses images, vérifier l'origine d'une vidéo, contacter les personnes concernées et confronter plusieurs sources deviennent des exigences encore plus essentielles. Publier rapidement ne doit jamais prendre le pas sur la nécessité d'informer justement. L'éducation aux médias et à l'information doit, elle aussi, intégrer cette nouvelle réalité. Les jeunes, les enseignants, les créateurs de contenus et les citoyens doivent apprendre à comprendre le fonctionnement des deepfakes, à reconnaître les manipulations possibles et surtout à suspendre leur jugement avant de partager. Car le véritable danger de cette révolution ne se limite pas à notre capacité à distinguer le vrai du faux. Il concerne aussi notre confiance collective dans l'information. Dans un monde où les yeux peuvent être trompés et les oreilles abusées, croire ne suffit plus. Il faut apprendre à vérifier. À l'ère des deepfakes, le réflexe le plus intelligent n'est peut-être pas de croire ce que l'on voit, mais de chercher à comprendre ce que l'on regarde. Cheikh Tidiane NDIAYE

items.title: Debate: ‘Lagos has waste-pick-and-dump system, not waste management’ – GRV
items.description: The governorship candidates of the Labour Party (LP), Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Funso Doherty, have criticised the Lagos State Government’s waste management system, describing it as inefficient and in need of urgent reform. The candidates made their positions known during the Lagos governorship debate in Lagos on Friday organised by the Nigeria Debate Consortium comprising Vanguard, Channels Television, TVC News, The PUNCH and TheCable. Rhodes-Vivour argued that waste management in Lagos was too centralised, with local governments having little or no involvement in the system. He said the state had failed to develop a waste-to-wealth value chain, relying instead on a system focused largely on collecting and dumping refuse. “The management of the system is too centralised. Local governments are not involved. We have failed to create a waste-to-wealth value chain. We don’t have a proper waste management system; we have a waste-pick-and-dump system,” he said. The LP candidate promised to decentralise waste management by involving local governments and creating opportunities to generate economic value from waste. “Under my government, that will change. We will get local governments involved. We will create value from waste, so that people, local governments and the state government can all benefit,” he added. Similarly, Doherty described the state’s waste management challenges as a failure of government, noting that while some parts of Lagos were clean, others continued to struggle with poor sanitation. “Parts of Lagos are smelling, while other parts are clean. We have a waste management problem, and I would characterise it as a failure of government,” he said. The NDC candidate identified inadequate investment in waste collection trucks as one of the factors worsening the situation. He also blamed the problem on the government’s approach to public services, arguing that successive administrations had increasingly withdrawn from the social sector while expecting private operators to fill the gap. “Part of the problem is that we don’t have enough investment in trucks. It goes back to the government stepping back from the social sector and wanting the private sector to do everything,” he added. items.title: Rejection, stigma drive some ex-convicts back to prison – Crime Check Foundation Director
items.description: The Executive Director of the Crime Check Foundation, Ibrahim Oppong Kwarteng, has attributed the return of some former prisoners to incarceration to societal rejection, stigma, and the difficulties they face in reintegrating into their communities after release. He said many ex-convicts struggle to rebuild their lives because they are often treated with suspicion and denied acceptance and opportunities, leaving some vulnerable to returning to prison. Speaking on JoyNews’ The Law programme on Sunday, November 8, Mr Kwarteng said the experiences of some former inmates who had repeatedly been in and out of prison highlighted the challenges associated with life after incarceration. He recalled that two former prisoners who shared their experiences on the programme had each been imprisoned three or four times, raising concerns about the circumstances that drive some people back into the correctional system. According to him, the uncertainty surrounding life after release, coupled with what he described as cultural rejection, makes it difficult for former inmates to establish themselves and become productive members of society. He argued that although former prisoners are expected to reform and reintegrate into their communities, the stigma attached to their past often undermines those efforts. Mr Kwarteng therefore called on the media to play a more active role in changing public perceptions of people who have served prison sentences. He said negative headlines, stereotyping and the continued labelling of former inmates could damage their confidence and make it harder for them to rebuild their lives. “I think those of us in the media have a huge responsibility to change the narrative,” he said. He added that meaningful reintegration would remain difficult unless the media reconsidered how it portrays former prisoners and stopped reinforcing negative stereotypes. “We need to change the media narrative, the stereotyping, the stigma if we want proper reintegration and reformation of ex-convicts,” he stressed. Mr Kwarteng warned that without adequate support, the country could continue to experience high levels of reoffending, referring to figures suggesting that about 30 per cent of former inmates return to prison. He, however, noted that the circumstances surrounding a former prisoner’s return should be examined carefully, arguing that not every case necessarily reflects a deliberate decision to engage in criminal activity again. He also raised concerns about the financial difficulties inmates face immediately after their release, particularly the limited support provided to help them return to their communities. According to him, the Ghana Prisons Service provides some released inmates with about GH¢15 to facilitate their journey home, an amount he believes is insufficient to meet their transportation needs. “How do you expect them to use GH¢15 to get to their destination?” he asked. He explained that returning to the larger society comes with several challenges, including finding accommodation, securing employment and overcoming the stigma associated with having a criminal record. The Crime Check Foundation Executive Director called for greater collaboration among government, the media and other relevant stakeholders to strengthen support systems for former prisoners. He also criticised what he described as the failure of successive governments to sustain adequate services and support for inmates, both during incarceration and after their release. Mr Kwarteng maintained that rehabilitation should not end when a prisoner walks out of the prison gates, insisting that meaningful reform requires deliberate efforts to ensure former inmates can secure livelihoods and regain acceptance in society. He said a more supportive approach would help reduce the barriers facing former prisoners and give them a better opportunity to rebuild their lives without returning to crime.

items.title: CAN U17 : la liste de Baha avec Akram Jadid et le talent de Chelsea Bilal Shah-Berkouz
items.description: Le sélectionneur national, Nabil Baha, qui encadre une 2è sélection U17 pour les tournois régionaux de qualification comme l'UNAF, a dévoilé sa liste en vue du tournoi de l'UNAF, qualificatif pour la prochaine Coupe d'Afrique des Nations U17. Cette échéance régionale cruciale se tiendra en Tunisie du 10 au 16 novembre prochains. Parmi les têtes d'affiche de cette convocation figure la sensation Akram Jadid. Âgé de seulement 15 ans et considéré comme un immense espoir au poste d'ailier gauche, le jeune joueur, déjà convié à s'entraîner avec l'équipe professionnelle de l'AC Milan en septembre dernier avant d'être appelé le mois suivant par Ahmed Kantari pour préparer le Mondial U17, honorera sa présence au sein du groupe. Le contingent s'enrichit également de la présence de Bilal Shah-Berkouz, milieu offensif de 16 ans évoluant au sein de l'académie de Chelsea. Le jeune pur-sang des Blues sera particulièrement attendu au tournant, d'autant que ses performances attireront l'attention après le passage en demi-teinte de son aîné en club, Ibrahim Rabbaj. Ce groupe sélectif marie habilement les talents de l'étranger et les pépites locales. Outre Jadid et Shah-Berkouz, l'armada d'expatriés intègre Damin el Fayda (Leipzig), Noham Varela (Brest), Rayan Kharmoud (Strasbourg), Ilyes Benane (Genk) ainsi que Mohammed Tatuh (Ajax). Ils viendront épauler les représentants de l'académie Mohammed VI de Football et des clubs nationaux, à l'instar de Sami Idahmad, Othmane Kam et Jad Jamila de la RS Berkane, Mohamed Reda Souni du FUS de Rabat, ainsi qu'Iyad Hamzi, Adam Souna, Aymane Aït Hammou et Younes Felloula. Les Lionceaux de l'Atlas entameront leur tournoi par un choc d'entrée face à l'Algérie, programmé dès le 10 novembre. Ils affronteront ensuite l'Égypte le 13 novembre avant de boucler leur parcours face au pays hôte, la Tunisie, le 16 du mois à Sousse. Bien que le Maroc soit déjà qualifié d'office pour la phase finale en tant que pays hôte, deux billets qualificatifs restent en jeu dans cette poule nord-africaine. Pour rappel, le calendrier de ces qualifications avait connu un premier report suite à l'intégration tardive du Maroc à la mi-septembre, avant que le forfait de la Libye ne soit officialisé cette semaine. Lors de la précédente campagne disputée au printemps dernier, les Marocains avaient survolé les débats en s’emparant de la première place du classement général avec un sans-faute étincelant de quatre victoires en autant de rencontres, dont un probant succès acquis face aux Algériens (3-0). The post CAN U17 : la liste de Baha avec Akram Jadid et le talent de Chelsea Bilal Shah-Berkouz appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .
