items.title: Can Beauty Make Us Good?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What is beauty? Is it really “in the eye of the beholder,” or is it an objective quality that exists in the world? Is it a mere decorative feature of life, or does it have something important to tell us? These are enduring human questions, but ones that the art world and the academic humanities—the natural custodians of beauty—gave up answering for a long time. In this episode, David Brooks talks to the Harvard professor Elaine Scarry, whose now-classic book On Beauty and Being Just brought the subject back to serious attention 25 years ago. David and Scarry discuss the ladder of loves, the universal appeal of symmetry, and why even prisoners at Guantánamo want to look at pretty pictures. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Today’s episode is about beauty. The basic thesis of this show is that in our society, we have massive forces of dehumanization trying to shrink us and beleaguered forces of humanization. Nothing could be more humanizing than beauty. We’re going to talk about how to cultivate a taste for beauty, how to create beauty, and we’re going to entertain the question: Does experiencing beauty make you a better person? My conversation partner today is Elaine Scarry, a very eminent literature professor, a humanist. She has a fancy title here at Harvard University, the Walter M. Cabot Professor of Aesthetics and the General Theory of Value, which is a fantastic professor title. Elaine wrote a very important book in 1999 called On Beauty and Being Just . It was an important moment because there was an assault on beauty and the very idea of beauty striking through the academy, through the art world. The idea is we shouldn’t create beauty. We should shock people into improving society. We should create ugly things to shock them. In 1999, Elaine rose up to defend beauty, and I would say 26 years later, she has carried the day. Beauty is back on the agenda in the academy, in the artistic world. You may notice that we are not at our usual set at Yale University today. We are at Harvard University. I want to reassure you that our podcast will not only be visiting colleges with gigantic endowments. We’ll be going to all sorts of places. I just happen to have a talk in Boston, so we thought we’d take advantage. I’m David Brooks, and this is The Permanent Questions . Brooks: Elaine Scarry, welcome to The Permanent Questions . Today we’re gonna talk about beauty, which you have—I don’t know if you’ve single-handedly rescued it in the academy, but you’ve done your part. I have to confess to you: I am an aesthetic Philistine. I recall when I wrote my first book, which was published in 2000, I wrote it in a dank, unfinished basement of my home with mildew and the smell of mildew everywhere. My desk was a plywood board, and my chair was a folding chair, and it was just me and my little laptop, and I was oblivious. I didn’t care. A lot of people were like, “I’m not working here.” But even I occasionally have these moments when you’re undone by something tremendously beautiful. I think the thing that strikes you about them is they lift you out of everyday reality for at least a brief time. You’ve done so much work on beauty; you must have had encounters of that sort with beauty. Scarry: I have had many encounters. I think that over time, the longer one lives, the more encounters one has, not just because they can keep accumulating and adding up, but because one learns to see or one becomes aware of just the astonishing plenitude that’s all around one. A kind of interesting analogy is what happens with color vision. John Dewey says that if you give small children the chance to learn color, it usually takes several years to be able to reliably identify a color. Whereas now researchers say that as adults, the average number of colors we can all see is 26,000, and if you count gray tones, it’s closer to a million. I think that something like that happens with beauty. You may not be aware of it as a child, or it may be happening to you, but you don’t have words for it. My partner and I often read books aloud. At one time, he was reading The Tale of Genji for about 20 minutes each morning. When he would begin to read, Lady Murasaki’s writing immediately lights up your mind. I would see pools of color that weren’t even directly prompted by what was said on the page. She’s writing about the court in Japan, but at the same time, Genji is always discovering beauty anywhere, in the outskirts and among poor people, and so forth. That kind of experience with reading is one that I’m sure we both have. Brooks: When you mentioned the ability to perceive more colors, there’s a neuroscientist at Northeastern named Lisa Feldman Barrett, who has a concept of emotional granularity. She says that some people can only experience very crude emotional categories. They know what’s an up state or a down state. But some people have the ability to distinguish between adjacent emotions like stress, anxiety, frustration, fear. They can make these fine gradations. Emotional granularity helps you read your own body, and maybe color granularity helps you see the world. I’m gonna quote you back to yourself: “Beautiful things have been placed here and there throughout the world to serve as small wake-up calls to perception, spurring lapsed alertness to its most acute level. Through its beauty, the world continually reconnects us to rigorous standard or perceptual care.” I like that phrase “perceptual care.” Perception isn’t just a passive process of opening our eyes and things come in. There’s something you can do to make yourself more perceptive or receptive toward beauty. Scarry: When you suddenly come face-to-face with something beautiful or it suddenly enters your world, you may have been thinking that you were fully awake and perceptive and listening and hearing and so forth, but one of the effects of beautiful things is to just really raise the level of perceptual acuity. It sets a new standard or a new bar, so that you realize that you should be giving that kind of attention to other things in the world that don’t necessarily come to you with such glory but that nonetheless deserve your attention. Brooks: It’s almost like an energy is being produced. I took my favorite drive in America two summers ago, down from Missoula, Montana, down the Salmon River to Salmon, Idaho. It is astoundingly beautiful. When I got out of the car, my wife and I were at some crappy hotel or something, and I’m buzzing with energy. If you see bluebirds in love, they’re bouncing all around each other. I look back almost with embarrassment at how excited I was to just have had this astonishing drive where you’re going through this valley, and every curve brings about a new scene. And it’s—you’re just energized, almost like puppy love or something. Scarry: There’s a wonderful poem by Seamus Heaney, I think it’s called “Postscript,” where he describes driving with his wife, Marie, along, I think it’s the west coast of Ireland, and the beauty of the wind and the water. And he says: No use in stopping the car. I find that same kind of event happens even when you’re moving through the world. Seamus Heaney’s poem ends by saying, It blows the heart open. I think that’s a very good description. Brooks: It’s a weird concept. It bleeds into everything. People perceive beauty in a million different forms. Yet we all call it one thing. We have a mutual friend, Brandon Vaidyanathan, who’s a sociologist at Catholic University. He did this big study of beauty, talking to scientists: “Are you motivated by beauty?” Some of them describe beauty in conventional terms, but some of them described beauty just as understanding. They are motivated by a beauty to understand, and they use that aesthetic language to describe just understanding an engineering problem or a math problem. Scarry: I’ve talked to scientists, and they do have different accounts. My friend Barry Mazur, who’s a mathematician, says that every solved theory is beautiful. It’s not that it has to be beautiful. It just happens to be the case that it is beautiful. Somebody else in the physics department who works on electromagnetic subjects says that he counsels his students, “Just because you’ve got a pretty theory, don’t think it’s true.” Whereas somebody I once spoke with at Yale who was in chemistry told me that he thinks that if a hypothesis is pretty or beautiful, it increases the chances that it’s true. So there’s really a wide range, from the one person who thinks, In every case, it’s beautiful, but there’s no reason why that should be , to somebody who actually thinks it predicts. Brooks: When we talk about a beautiful landscape, a beautiful face, a beautiful equation, are we talking about the same thing? What is the core concept here? Scarry: I think we’re definitely talking about the same thing, even though there’s tremendous variation, and certainly variation in the things that most strike people as beautiful. But one thing that they all share, which is foregrounded in the math example, is the idea of symmetry or proportion. It’s just so deeply there. I think of a text that I love that really makes that clear, St. Augustine’s “De Musica,” where he’s talking about equality as a feature of God, and he talks about the fact that you can see it in human faces. You can see it in dance steps. You can hear it in music. He even gives examples like a cake or feeling the softness of another person’s body—that what you’re feeling is equality, which isn’t normally how we would think of smooth skin, but he says that’s equality that you’re experiencing. It’s startling. He’s not making a plea for democracy, but he is talking about proportion. He even says, by the way, that color—like the color of your jacket, the fact that it’s a uniform blue, or the sky is, at least in patches, a uniform blue—is an example of equality and the tremendous pleasure that brings. When you hear scientists—like one scientist who’s written a book about beauty in science is named Mario Livio, and every example he gives has got startling symmetry in it. There are other features as well. For example, intensity and vibrancy. I think that the quality of aliveness is absolutely key in all the examples. Brooks: Do you think that our sense of beauty is somewhat evolutionarily baked in? Symmetry probably has some survival advantages. You want people who have symmetrical faces, and people look at body shapes for fertility signs. That suggests there’s some universal sense of what beauty is, that all humans would see the same face and think, “Oh, that’s beautiful.” Scarry: I sometimes have people say to me, “Well, there are famous faces, famous models who have a kind of asymmetry in their face.” That’s true, but it’s a .00001 asymmetry. The important thing to realize, as you said in your description, is that if a face is really nonsymmetrical, there’s no way that it can be in the neighborhood of beauty. By the way, I think that is a partial answer to your question about evolution. Yes, it may be that we’re like butterflies and birds. It’s been said of butterflies and birds that they keep getting more and more extravagant because the females choose the males on the basis of their beauty and so forth. There is probably some kind of reproductive bias, which might also be true of human beings. But I think that part of the reason that beauty is so important to us is because it is opposed to injury. It makes us deeply averse to injury. It acts on us so that when we see someone who’s injured, we know the first thing you have to do is try to repair it. It makes us, or should make us, hesitant about inflicting injuries on others. How could you survive as a species if you didn’t, overall, have a kind of aversion to acts of inflicting injury? Brooks: I want to get to the relationship between beauty and morality in a minute because I think that’s a central subject here. But I want to stay on the experience of beauty just a little longer. You use a word that I’d like to hear you expand upon. You say beauty is “lifesaving.” What do you mean by that? Scarry: Here’s an amazing fact that I learned relatively recently. In the early ’80s, a researcher i n Sweden looked at the people in hospital who were recovering from surgery, and half of them had a window that looked out onto a green grove, and the other half had a window that looked out onto a brick wall. And those in the room with the green window got better much more quickly. It makes you realize that we might not have it right about what beauty is, but we better try and get it right, if it actually leads to people being able to more quickly recover. Every couple of years, the American Society of Civil Engineers gives a report card to our bridges, our highways, our levies, and among other things, our public schools. I just looked at the one for 2025 because I knew I was gonna be speaking with you. And though the general drift of the whole overall report card is to go up—I think the overall grade in 2025 went up from a C- to a C. The public school, and they’re talking not about teachers, but about the physical environment, they give the grade of D+. Brooks: When I read that lifesaving line, I thought of someone I admire a great deal, which is Tina Turner, the singer. Her story is really built around beauty. She really had this sense. She grew up in Nutbush, Tennessee, to a dad who left her and a mom who was somewhat narcissistic and also left her, and she could sing. And so this guy Ike Turner finds her; realizes, That’s my million dollars ; and basically enslaves her. He doesn’t pay her. He beats her savagely. He commits adultery on a mass scale, has mistresses living in their house with them. Just a brutal life. The wedding that he proposed—took her down to Tijuana, no dress, no kiss, just a civil ceremony, and then he took her to a whorehouse and made her watch a sex show. Her life was just brutal under him. And at one point, she attempts suicide. She’s ready to go. She wakes up in the hospital. Ike is furious at her for upsetting his budgetary plans. But then she decides, “What did I want when I was a girl?” She always loved beauty. And so she started doing these Buddhist practices and doing floral decorations and keeping a journal. She built herself up to be the kind of person who could stand up to Ike Turner, and it took her 14 years. But she eventually fought back, and eventually ran away, had her own career, became a superstar, age 60, a sexy rockstar lady. Then she got remarried, and at her wedding, she insisted there be 100,000 roses. When I read 100,000, I went, “That’s a lot of roses.” That must’ve cost a fortune. But she had rebuilt her life on the basis of creating beauty. And as a rebuttal to her first Tijuana wedding, she was gonna have 100,000 roses. Scarry: You can destroy all fairness. It sounds like her husband had managed to completely eliminate any sense of fairness in their household. It’s hard to completely eliminate beauty. There’s often something flying by the window. Once when I was in Geneva and talking with the International Red Cross, one of the Red Cross workers said that she had asked a prisoner at Guantánamo if there was anything she could bring him, because that’s often something the Red Cross offers. One prisoner said that he would like a photograph of a flower. Another example of Tina Turner’s solution to the problem she was in, where you’re really trying to make yourself believe that there still is symmetry and vivacity in the world. I was once at a conference in England, and there was a young woman who had studied Romanian prisons. It was a women’s prison that she was studying. The women would take tiny little threads from their undergarments and weave little tapestries one inch by one inch and give them to each other. They treasured that and survived by means of it. Brooks: Maybe this is wrong, but it seems to me it’s not quite controllable, that you can put yourself in the way of beauty, but you can’t say, “I am about to be overwhelmed by beauty the next time I walk down the street.” Scarry: There are reliably beautiful sources that one can go to. Like returning to Tolstoy’s War and Peace or going to a particular street that you loved in your childhood. But often the beauty does also suddenly vanish. I usually teach a graduate course on beauty, but occasionally I’ve taught a freshman seminar on beauty, and at one point one of the freshman who was very interested in the beauty of design, in an iPhone, for example, surmised that the fact that beauty often doesn’t last forever—it might last three seconds, it might last three years, but it often goes away—then leads us, as I wrote in the book On Beauty and Being Just , to the act of creation. It’s a kind of instigation of creation and a kind of passing on of beauty. So you could say we compensate for the brevity of beautiful things or the short life of flowers, or you could say it’s actually an okay thing that it’s so short because that instigates our own acts of creation. Brooks: One more piece of the perception of beauty that strikes me as incredibly important these days is amor mundi— love the world. Imagine if we were surrounded by nature that was hideously ugly. We would feel alienated from the world; we would feel this is not a home. The fact that it is a beautiful place makes us feel at home and love the world. You quoted Augustine. I love Augustine, so I’m going to quote him: “I asked the Earth, I asked the sea and the deeps. Among the living animals and the things that creep, I asked the winds that blow, I asked the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and to all things that stand at the door of my flesh. My question was the gaze I turned to them. Their answer was their beauty.” Augustine is such a poet, but one of the things that strikes me as important: I’ve been at three different colleges in the past week, and at each college, the students in front of me, not with my participation, got in an argument about how rotten the world is. A lot of them think it’s completely rotten, whether climate change, AI, or everything, just the whole world’s been ruined for them. Some think it only marginally rotten. That rotten-world syndrome—they may be right, they may be wrong, but it’s not a positive way to go through life. If you want to change the world, it seems to me you want to love the world. I think the beauty of the world makes us feel at home. There is a sort of homecoming feeling about beauty that makes you think, Yeah, this is my home. This is the beautiful place that I get to spend my life . Without that, it’s almost hard to have hope. Scarry: One of my students, long ago, back in the 1990s, said, “Beauty restores your trust in the world.” So you can be attending to very harsh things, and suddenly you see something, and it restores your belief in the world. Now, I do think students are really facing a triple decker of problems. And yet, like you, I think, How can we even have a planet this beautiful? Is it just that we’re designed to appreciate it? Those other planets, by the way—has anyone actually noticed what they look like? The Earth is almost incomprehensible in how beautiful it is. But I think that, gradually, students will be sensitive to that and will feel some kind of resilience about what’s happening. Brooks: When I talk about the students, they’re always the hero in my story. Today’s students have been put in a very challenging circumstance, and they’re fighting back the best they can. But I sometimes think they are too pessimistic about the world, and I say, “Read history.” What decade would you go back to? Things have always been pretty rotten. Before we leave this, I just want to ask you about one concept that I know very little about. I had a friend who was an opera singer who was a fan of duende , the kind of beauty that’s intermingled with sadness. We can all think of songs and poems that embody this. What strikes me about this whole conversation—we’ve had the perception of beauty. You can go through life with a very utilitarian frame of mind. It’s all material. And what beauty does is it reminds you the world is not strictly a utilitarian, material place. There’s an enchantment, at least in our perception of it. Scarry: Many, many poems, or the music you’re describing, might be about subjects that are sad. Like the passing of the year in Keats’s ode “To Autumn” that’s also so unbelievably gorgeous. Or many elegies that are obviously full of sadness, and yet are very beautiful. Aquinas says that even something ugly if rendered in a beautiful artwork can be beautiful. Brooks: I was at my folks’ home, and they had some guests coming over from France, and there was a woman from Paris. This was her first trip to New York. And they said, “How’d you find it?” And I love New York. I’m a New Yorker. But she said, “Well, I didn’t realize it’d be so ugly.” And I was like, “It is kind if ugly, but the ugly parts are the parts I like.” If you love the ugly parts of your place, you love the place. Scarry: I guess you have to find a good path in, because usually when I’m coming in, I get out at LaGuardia, and it just seems like I’m always coming down a very tree-lined street with brownstones, and I think, “This is a very beautiful city.” But your story puts me in mind of a friend who always loved New York, who went to Rome, and suddenly would have nothing more to say good about New York. Brooks: Washington, D.C., where I live, is supposed to be Paris. When we go to Paris, I think, Oh, we’ve got a long way to go . I’m not endorsing Donald Trump’s arch, by the way. I ran across the work of an anthropologist named Ellen Dissanayake, and she wrote a book called Homo Aestheticus . She makes the claim that human beings have a natural desire to make special, and she means to make special sacred occasions, to—when you go to a fancy party, you dress up. You want to make it special. When my wife gets home, the first thing she does is get out her Trader Joe’s flowers, which she has just bought. She lights eight million candles. She sets the table even though she hasn’t cooked the meal yet. She wants to make the occasion special. This is something in us. We want to have special occasions, rituals, and we use beauty to create them. It seems to me like that’s what a wedding is all about, or anything else. I don’t know what you make of this impulse towards specialness. Scarry: Well, it sounds immediately convincing. One recognizes it in practice, and also, I think, I understand how it works. Given the tremendous pleasure that beauty brings, you just want people to have that pleasure when they can. There’s a statement by Kant, who says that a lot of different things give pleasure, but they have an end point. You’re hungry, you have a good meal, and so forth. But he says that the pleasure of beauty is inexhaustible. You never get tired of it. You never have enough. Brooks: This reminds me, you’ve also done some work in your career on Boethius. I was reading his book The Consolation of Philosophy . He’s got a passage on what you should orient your life toward. If you want money, you’ll always feel poor. If you want power, you’ll always feel weak. If you want status, you will always be the victim of other people’s opinions. So he’s really saying, “Don’t want these finite goods. Want infinite goods.” There’s a famous commencement address by David Foster Wallace at Kenyon College, where he says, Everybody worships, but if you worship money and power and status, you’ll always feel inadequate. If you worship looks, you’ll die a thousand deaths before they bury you. When I read that David Foster Wallace speech, which I’ve read many times before, I thought, “He must have read Boethius.” Scarry: He probably did. Brooks: But it is a good way to orient our lives. If you orient toward finite things, you will run out. But beauty, belonging, competence, respect, significance, meaning—these things are infinite goods. It’s probably a good idea to orient your life toward the infinite ones, because you’ll never run to the end of them. And so it was strange that it became the model, and even stranger was the fact that it began to be said even about inanimate objects. You’re going to paint and you’re just reifying the paintings by standing there looking at them. You think, But aren’t the paintings made to be looked at? Brooks: This must have grown to some degree out of feminist thinking that the male gaze was objectifying. Scarry: Absolutely it grew out of that. And it’s not as though people who were complaining about the male gaze are necessarily wrong. But the effect, it was to begin to blanket everything. And you would be sitting in a seminar where of course you want to look at one another, and you’re talking about how lethal it is to look. So that was one thing. The other thing was the idea that there’s a lot of problems in the world, and it’s diverting our attention away from those problems. And there’s no way that you could ever convince me that by attending to beauty you become less aware of problems. To me, they are opposite ends of a pole, and when you are in the presence of something beautiful, it’s helping to nourish your recognition of what is intolerable, and cruelty is intolerable. And vice versa. When you see cruelty, you long for, as at Guantánamo, the photograph of the flower. So I think they were incoherent arguments, and I think that they were also mutually exclusive. On the one hand, one argument was saying, “Our acts of vision are destructive. You hurt the thing you’re looking at.” The other argument was that by not looking at something, by ignoring something, you produce harm in it. And even if you go to the locus of the problem, the idea that there are cases, let’s say, when the male gaze is used violently, even then it is something that can’t plausibly be generalized to males looking at women or women looking at men. Because if you go back through time, it’s the perceiver who’s always vulnerable. It’s Dante whose knees are buckling when he sees Beatrice. That occurs all the way down the line. It’s like Sappho’s “Raise high the roof beam, carpenters.” You have to make the doorways taller to accommodate the person. You have to fill the hillside with flowers. It goes back to the earlier conversation we were having about the kind of growth or enlargement of perception that comes by being in the presence of beauty. Brooks: There’s one other argument that the war on beauty folks could wage; I see it in my own profession in journalism. There are two things going on. One is middle-class Americans or the bourgeoisie are overly content, and you need to shock them out of their mediocrity. And the other is that in the media, our theory of change is if we can explain what’s wrong, we’ve done our job. We have a strong bias toward negative news. And we don’t have to explain how to fix it. We just expose the sin. And I think it’s been proven that this approach to promoting social change by shocking people or by reminding them of how awful things are is a pretty rotten way to motivate people to do change. You can’t just say, “This is rotten, this is hopeless, this is terrible.” You have to provide an alternative vision, which is what beauty is—literally an alternative vision. Scarry: I agree with that. In fact, have you seen this new documentary called Josh’s Wedding ? You watch the computer generate its own poem. Then you also see it give its opinion of human beings, which is that we’re contemptible, we’re small, we’re worthless. Perhaps that is just one of 1,000 things that AI would say about human beings. But it suddenly began to make me and Philip Fisher, my life partner, worry: “Wait a minute, these computers are being trained on all these books and newspapers that report only the negative.” For every act of cruelty, there are probably that day a million acts of kindness in the world. The kind of fear that AI might inflict cruelty by unleashing a nuclear weapon or whatever always seemed odd to me, only in the sense of: What would be the motive? But if the picture we have of ourselves is so negative, that might be a reason. Brooks: You published this book, 26 years ago? And when you did it, the anti-beauty movement was at full force. Scarry: I think that’s right. Brooks: What’s the update 26 years later? Scarry: I think that gradually things have been restored. I mean, I see conferences on beauty. I think that students—you know, even in the ’90s I taught this course on beauty, in the ’90s, and certainly students took the course. There are lots of signs that that is much less of a problem. Now, somebody who is in art history told me that that is still the case in art history departments. But I didn’t question him enough to know if that is absolutely the case. I just know that it’s something that I shouldn’t so blithely think, Yeah, we’re out of it now . We’re out of danger now . Maybe we’re not. Brooks: These things take a while. As they say, intellectual history travels by hearse. You have to lose people to lose certain ideas. Well, thank you for this time. I’m reminded of a friend of mine named Jenny McShane, who I’ve known since I was 10, made a movie called The Quilters about guys in a maximum-security prison who quilt. And that’s the center of their life. And they’re in there, they’re never coming out, and they just wanna create beauty. Among people like that, beauty never went out of fashion. Elaine Scarry, thank you so much for joining us on The Permanent Questions . Scarry: Thank you so much for having me. Brooks: I leave this conversation just reminded again that beauty is everywhere. We talk about moral beauty, physical beauty, intellectual beauty, mathematical beauty, a beautiful tennis shot, and I really was persuaded by Elaine that it is all one thing. Beauty is one thing, one sensation of symmetry, of reciprocity, of just something that’s innately pleasurable. I’m also reminded that perception is so much of what we do. We used to have this idea that perception, you just open your eyes and reality floods in, and the real mental action up here was thinking, was cognition, cogitation. But I think we’re understanding as the cognitive sciences bring us along that perception is thinking, and most of our thinking is actually in our perceptions. You don’t have to think about whether you’re seeing a morally admirable act or a morally degrading act. You just see it and you know immediately in the way you know a painting is beautiful or not beautiful. And so I think we got a little glimpse on that process. And then I really walk away persuaded that even though I can think of a lot of artists and poets who are not wonderful human beings, I do think the constant act of experiencing beauty over years, over decades, does enlarge the soul and does make us kinder toward others, more considerate toward others, and greater in our longing for the good. So thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Elaine Scarry. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic in partnership with Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions drop each Sunday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, on Spotify, on Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you wanna support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. See you next week. The Permanent Questions is edited by Christopher Beha and produced by Rebecca Davis. This episode was engineered by Miguel Carrascal. Our theme is by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

items.title: The Secret Ingredient to Mac and Cheese
items.description: My Aunt Louise and my grandmother both smoked Virginia Slims. At social events, even barbecues, Louise’s cigarette was in a theater-length holder. She was married to a loud man we called Uncle Benny, who held his Marlboro in the same hand as his highball. Louise’s kitchen, with its Talavera tile and swinging door, functioned like a VIP suite. It’s where the mac and cheese was made, and the very important people were the kids. This was late-1970s Los Angeles. Louise and Benny lived in a gray Spanish-revival bungalow common to the multiracial Miracle Mile: a red-clay roof and a front courtyard tinkling with chimes. On any given weekend, a hunting pal of Benny’s might stomp onto Louise’s spotless back patio with just-caught cod, or crayfish still moving in the trap—maybe even deer heart, thawing in a ziplock, or fresh pheasant to throw on the grill. It was fine for others to contribute a protein, but side dishes were Louise’s domain: deviled eggs, braised mustard greens, and the mac and cheese for which she was famous. I’d watch Louise fold boiled elbow noodles into the Cracker Barrel Extra Sharp I had shredded, plus eggs beaten with Knudsen whole milk (as opposed to Carnation evaporated). There were other ingredients—a spoonful of dry mustard, a pinch of Tony Chachere’s Original Creole Seasoning—but what stood out to me were Louise’s careful shakes, from a Schilling tin, of cream of tartar. I didn’t know what that was, and I wasn’t alone. For Louise’s clique, cream of tartar was a culinary idiosyncrasy. “Cream of what?” they’d ask. “Why?” Now, decades later, rowdy debates about mac and cheese are all over social media, especially at holiday time. Should mac and cheese be pourable, or baked until it can be cut like brownies? Is truffle a grace note, or too highfalutin? The sparring goes down in TikTok Stitches and the comment sections of Instagram Reels, as creators mix in mozzarella or mascarpone. Home cooks zhuzh up boxes of Kraft. My Haitian American friends make macaroni au gratin with habanero-laced epis . Ina Garten marinates her cooked pasta in cream , as you would overnight oats. I adore a good, melty cube of Velveeta (in my scrambled eggs), but using Campbell’s Condensed Cheddar Cheese Soup? In mac and cheese? Gag me—as we used to say in 1980s Southern California—with a spoon. Alex Hill , an L.A.-based content creator and recipe developer under the name @justaddhotsauce, knows that ingredients and cooking styles go in and out of fashion. She grew up watching her mother learn to make mac and cheese from the singer Patti LaBelle, a best-selling cookbook author whose recipe is a five-cheese stunner (and made in the custard style of my Aunt Louise). Hill’s mom, a Puerto Rican married to a Black American, wanted to make mac and cheese in a way beloved by her husband and his family. “I thought my mom made the best mac and cheese,” Hill, whose own mac is béchamel-based, told me. “She used Velveeta. And now it’s so taboo.” My Aunt Louise was not kin but sister-friend to my maternal grandmother, Lottie. They were glamorous, frank, and 40 years older than me, but Louise spoke about the body in a way that shared DNA often disallows. When I was 12, she told me there was no way to grate cheese without risking the skin of my knuckles. “Stop being so tentative,” Louise said. “As you know, it’s not if you bleed, kiddo. It’s when .” I had thought that the way Louise looked out for me and other children meant that I knew her. I’ll never know how much I didn’t know. My grandmother and her girlfriends came of age in 1940s California, when school segregation was customary (and legal, until ’47). Aunt Louise and Grandma Lottie both married military men and lived through the assassination era. I used to think of these women as always being braced for something. Tense. As we all got older, I could see they were shoring up a broken heart. People in my grandmother’s set rarely talked about their emotions, at least to us. They were who they were because things were the way they were. Like Louise, my grandmother was a good cook who did not love to cook. But Grandma taught me to make a nog so thick with beaten egg whites that it’s eaten with a spoon. When I realized that she didn’t even like the nog, she told me that you don’t have to like something to make it. “You can make it,” she said, “because other people like it.” (I hear this in my head when I make my “famous” peach cobbler that I don’t even like. Compliments are yummy, though, right? Especially when you’re hungry for them.) Cooking for pleasure must have been a complex notion for my grandmother; her mother had cooked for a living in the Piedmont area of Oakland, where Black people were forbidden to be owners or tenants. At one of Louise and Benny’s gatherings—where spatchcocked birds dripped with browned butter, brown sugar, and cayenne—I heard one of Louise’s friends getting nosy about the menu. This friend’s name was Mae or Bea, something one-syllable, and she was among the fools Louise welcomed but did not suffer, when it came to kitchen meddling. Mae (or Bea): You’re not making a roux? Louise: Roux is for gumbo and gravy. Then one of Benny’s crew barreled through the swinging door with charred wild-turkey thighs. Before Louise could block him, the man stuffed a boy’s mouth with a burnt piece, then howled: “That’s a rabbit! That’s the Easter Bunny you just ate!” Now that child was crying. Then another. I wanted to fight this man. But I was 12. In that kitchen, with its undernotes of Clorox, Louise looked up from dotting margarine on the steaming noodles in her rectangular glass pan. She didn’t like grown men “hooting and hollering.” She didn’t like jokes that only the joker found funny. Aunt Louise had spoken to me of the sourness among folks who experienced different levels of possibility, and freedom. This was why she didn’t much like for the generations to mix—unless she was on duty at the velvet rope. So Louise hustled me, my sister, and our pals into her den. She passed me, the oldest, a boxy television remote, then fanned out editions of Ebony , Life , Essence , and Sunset . She brought us a bowl of chips and some mild salsa. Shutting the door as she left, Louise gave us a look that said simply and seriously that this was our territory while treacherous guests were nearby. As usual, I followed her back to the kitchen. I noted how Louise contained the chaos. I was brave before the deer’s heart. I got back to cheese grating. In the summer of 2000, when my sister was getting married, I visited Louise in a nursing home. She was a widow recovering—to the degree that she ever could—from an amputation. I had been living in New York City for seven years, and she acted as if that were a magical distance and length of time. My grandmother had told her I was doing well in my work—that I was, like the Jeffersons, moving on up. With a wink, Louise gave me a bottle of Rive Gauche from her bureau, and then asked me if I still cooked. I said I did, and I was glad it was true. “I think we’re losing recipes,” Alex Hill had said, and for more than mac and cheese. Recipes aren’t just nourishment, nor are they merely strokes of “culture.” They are relationships. They make us feel included and protected. For me, they are loyalty—a sweetness where there might have been bitters. Hill, who has a cookbook coming out next year, knows the necessity of sharing her passions on social media, but she doesn’t want to cook something solely because it might go viral. “I actually want to cook ,” she said. “I want you to cook my recipes.” The elbows in Aunt Louise’s mac and cheese held cooked milk in their curves. My recipe is not the same as Louise’s, but it’s close. I use cream of tartar. I believe roux is for gumbo and gravy. I tilt my glass pan, just as Louise did, to see if any liquid moves. If it doesn’t, I pull it from the oven. The top, crunchy. The edges, brown. Our custard, silky. Alex Hill says cream of tartar is a stabilizer. Louise had told me that too, in her Miracle Mile courtyard. “Cream of tartar has no taste,” she said. “It just holds everything together.” At the time, I didn’t understand. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “The Right Way to Make Mac and Cheese .”

items.title: Mandiana : le directeur préfectoral de l’Environnement accusé d’avoir perçu 105 millions GNF pour renoncer à un contrôle minier
items.description: 105 millions de francs guinéens contre l'absence de contrôle. C'est l'accusation grave portée par des responsables locaux de Balandougouba contre le directeur préfectoral de l'Environnement de Mandiana et son équipe, soupçonnés d'avoir monnayé leur mission dans les zones d'exploitation aurifère. Le mis en cause rejette en bloc et menace de porter plainte. Une affaire de corruption présumée secoue la sous-préfecture de Balandougouba, dans la préfecture de Mandiana. Au cœur de la controverse : une somme de 105 millions de francs guinéens qui aurait été collectée auprès de plusieurs villages à la suite de discussions avec une mission du service préfectoral de l'Environnement. Selon les témoignages recueillis auprès d'un participant aux discussions et du maire de Balandougouba, les faits remontent à une mission conduite dans la localité par des agents de l'Environnement, sous la direction du directeur préfectoral. D'après ces témoignages, les présidents de districts auraient exprimé leur opposition à l'entrée de la mission dans les zones minières, par crainte de voir les équipements utilisés pour l'exploitation de l'or détruits ou endommagés. Une inquiétude liée, selon eux, aux opérations de répression menées dans la préfecture voisine de Siguiri. C'est dans ce contexte que des discussions auraient été engagées entre les responsables locaux, les Tombolamas et le maire pour trouver une issue à la situation. 105 millions GNF collectés dans plusieurs villages Dans son témoignage, notre source locale affirme que ces discussions ont abouti à une collecte d'argent auprès de plusieurs villages. Il explique que la première proposition aurait consisté à réunir 20 millions de francs guinéens par village, un montant jugé trop élevé. Après de nouvelles concertations, un compromis aurait été trouvé autour de 15 millions GNF pour les grands villages, notamment Balandougouba-centre, Kinienkoura, Faragbèkoro et Sidikila. Les villages disposant de moins d'équipements miniers auraient, quant à eux, contribué à hauteur de 5 millions GNF. « Le maire nous a demandé de faire la somme totale. Elle était de 105 millions. C'est ce que nous avons payé pour leur donner », affirme t-il Il précise que, pour les contributeurs, cet argent devait permettre aux exploitants de poursuivre leurs activités. Il ajoute qu'après cette collecte, les participants auraient reçu la consigne de garder le silence sur l'affaire. « Ils nous ont dit, comme nous avons fini de payer, de dire aux nôtres de maîtriser leurs bouches. Nous aussi, nous avons accepté cela », soutient-il. Le témoin affirme également que, malgré ces versements présumés, les activités minières auraient été sommées de s'arrêter dès le lendemain du départ de la mission. Le maire apporte sa version des faits Le maire de Balandougouba confirme l'existence de discussions entre les responsables locaux et la mission de l'Environnement. Il explique avoir convoqué les présidents de districts et les Tombolamas après avoir été informé de l'arrivée des agents, qui lui auraient annoncé une opération de répression. Selon son récit, les responsables de districts ne souhaitaient pas que les agents pénètrent dans les zones minières, redoutant notamment la destruction des machines utilisées pour l'exploitation de l'or. Le maire affirme que les discussions se sont poursuivies de 10 heures à 21 heures. Il soutient que les Tombolamas auraient ensuite été chargés de réunir de l'argent dans l'espoir d'obtenir un changement de décision. Il apporte toutefois une précision importante : selon lui, le directeur préfectoral de l'Environnement aurait initialement refusé de recevoir cette somme. « De 17 heures jusqu'à 21 heures, ils tentaient de lui donner l'argent, mais il a dit que sa personnalité ne lui permettait pas de prendre l'argent. Il a déclaré qu'il était venu pour la répression et qu'il ferait la répression le lendemain », rapporte le maire. Il affirme avoir finalement plaidé auprès du responsable de la mission, qui aurait accepté de céder sur certains points, tout en maintenant qu'il n'avait pas demandé d'argent et qu'il souhaitait effectuer sa visite de terrain. Le directeur rejette les accusations et menace de porter plainte Joint par téléphone, le directeur préfectoral de l'Environnement de Mandiana a vivement contesté les informations qui lui ont été rapportées. Rejetant toute implication dans une éventuelle perception d'argent, il a estimé que de telles accusations devaient être étayées par des preuves concrètes. Il a annoncé son intention d'engager une procédure judiciaire contre les auteurs de ces déclarations. « Pour un premier temps, il va falloir que je porte plainte […] Moi, je vais porter plainte aujourd'hui », a-t-il déclaré. Le responsable a également invité le journaliste à se rendre sur le terrain afin de vérifier les faits et de réunir les éléments justificatifs nécessaires. Au cours de cet échange, le directeur a également évoqué certaines initiatives de son service à Mandiana, notamment des activités de reboisement et une cérémonie organisée à l'occasion de la Journée mondiale des éléphants. Il a regretté, selon ses propos, que les actions positives de son service ne bénéficient pas de la même attention que les accusations portées contre lui. Plusieurs questions restent sans réponse Au-delà de ces déclarations contradictoires, plusieurs interrogations demeurent : les 105 millions de francs guinéens ont-ils effectivement été collectés et remis ? Qui en aurait été le véritable destinataire ? La mission de l'Environnement a-t-elle finalement renoncé à certaines opérations de contrôle à la suite des discussions ? Pour l'heure, les témoignages recueillis constituent des accusations qui restent à vérifier. De son côté, le directeur préfectoral de l'Environnement conteste les faits qui lui sont imputés et réclame des preuves. À Mandiana, cette affaire relance le débat sur le contrôle des activités minières, la protection de l'environnement et les conditions d'application des mesures de répression dans les zones d'exploitation aurifère de Balandougouba. Karifa Doumbouya, correspondant régional – Kankan L’article Mandiana : le directeur préfectoral de l'Environnement accusé d'avoir perçu 105 millions GNF pour renoncer à un contrôle minier est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: KP plans to set up faceless ATCs, spend Rs70bn on CTD and police in a year as part of counterterrorism initiatives
items.description: The administrative setup in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa plans to establish faceless anti-terrorism courts in the province as part of its initiatives to strengthen the fight against terrorism, according to a briefing by the officials televised on Sunday. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi was also present at the briefing, where KP Secretary Home Amjad Ali Khan outlined several measures planned to step up the fight against terrorism and explained that witnesses in terrorism cases feared coming forward. “So, we have recently sent the amendment to set up faceless anti-terrorism courts. Through this, not just the protection of witnesses, but that of prosecutors and judges will also be ensured,” he said. Moreover, he said the administrative setup planned to spend Rs70 billion on the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and police in a year, in order to increase their capacity. Talking about dealing with terrorism in the policy domain, Khan noted that in the past there had been a “lack of political ownership” in the fight against terrorism in the province. “Our armed forces and law enforcement agencies are making sacrifices in the war against terrorism; however, [..] the provincial government was not taking ownership for them.” The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. Khan stressed the need for a “close liaison” on terrorism between the public, political leadership, and security forces. He further recalled that despite the Centre formulating an Afghan policy, “actions continued to be taken in the province contrary to that policy, leading to confusion among the people”. He also noted that there was “propaganda against the security forces in attempts to sabotage the counterterrorism efforts in the province”. The official then spoke of the “insufficient funding” for civil law enforcement agencies (LEAs), including police and CTD, particularly in the merged districts, where he said only 3.2 per cent of the budget was allocated for security. He highlighted a shortage of over 10,000 personnel in the police, while also noting the lack of security infrastructure. “Along with that, in the merged districts, most of the dependence regarding the police force is on former ex-Fata Khasadars and Levies,” he said, adding that the police personnel did not receive adequate training. He further highlighted inadequate counter-drone protection, for which the available system was at a capacity of 12pc, noting that terrorists were using drone technology as well, “due to which we are suffering considerable losses”. He also highlighted the lack of adequate Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) teams. “Because of these issues [..] we have suffered significant losses over the past two or three years in which 1,003 personnel of the armed forces were martyred, 627 police personnel, and 808 civilian casualties occurred,” he stated. Referring to the Centre’s Rs160bn package for uplift of KP, Khan said that the provincial set-up and the federal government were on the same page, expressing hope that “its effects will be seen in the coming days”. He went on to outline plans to strengthen police capacity in the province, including fortifying sensitive police stations and check posts, extending the Safe City project, and establishing anti-drone systems in Dera Ismail Khan, Lakki Marwat, and Bannu as well as functionalising District Nerve Centres in ten districts. Updated information will be available to LEAs from the centres, he added. Under the legal interventions in policing, the official said that faceless ATC courts will be set up. “Witnesses in terrorism cases are afraid to come forward due to their identity. So we have recently sent the amendment for these faceless courts. Through this measure, witnesses, prosecutors, and judges will have their protection ensured,” he stated. Detailing the technical abilities of the police, the official said that satellite communication systems were being set up in areas with no prior communication system. He added that the provincial administration was also deploying AI tools for social media monitoring to counter terrorists’ narrative. Khan also stressed the need for increased public outreach, including strengthening District Dispute Resolution Councils as well as establishing tribal liaison committees. “Regular jirgas will be held with notables, regular interaction will occur with the public, and community mobilisation will take place,” he stated. He also outlined plans for police to be trained in modern technology such as anti-drone systems and sniping. He also recalled the provincial setup’s decision to revise packages for martyred police personnel. Khan continued: “Kinetic operations will be scaled up so that militancy can be eliminated. In this regard, intelligence-based operations will be enhanced, area sanitisation will be carried out [..], terrorist facilitators will be arrested, and re-verification will also be carried out for people on the fourth schedule to ensure none of them is providing facilitation or support to terrorists. He also added that the Rapid Response Force will be mobilised. Khan added that the provincial administration also planned to increase the number of police check posts. He announced that the government was spending Rs70bn on CTD and police annually. “In this regard, the police are being given Rs59.8bn, of which Rs33.4bn will be for their infrastructure and Rs26.4bn will be for procurement, while Rs10.3bn is being given to the CTD, of which Rs5.4bn is for infrastructure, and Rs4.9bn for procurement.” He added that police surveillance capacity — at 15pc presently — will be increased to 60pc, while for CTD it will be enhanced by 70pc. “The police’s counter-aerial threat capacity, which is currently at 1pc, will be taken up to 50pc. Our air strike capability is currently at 18pc and will be increased to 50pc, as well as night fighting capacity, with vehicle armour capacity of the police to be improved by 45pc,” the official said. He added that “jammer availability was at 40pc but will be increased to 50pc while counter-drone capability — at 52pc presently — will be increased to 60pc”. Protective gear and vehicle availability will be improved as well, while specialised training will be held in collaboration with the Pakistan Armed Forces. The official also announced action against smuggling, narcotics, extortion and non-custom-paid vehicles. “The purpose of all these measures is to provide a safe and secure environment to the people of KP where they can spend their lives, according to their codes and traditions,” Khan concluded. Since the imposition of the governor’s rule in KP, the provincial administration has vowed to steer the province towards development and eliminate terrorism. Chairing his first apex committee meeting after taking charge of the province, governor Kundi promised to equip police and CTD with resources. “Whatever weapons you want, whatever you need, we will get them to you. We will not compromise on our police officers and personnel. We will equip them well,” Kundi had said at the meeting. Last month, he also announced an increase in the compensation packages for police officers martyred or injured in the line of duty. Governor Kundi calls for ownership of war against terrorism Speaking at the occasion, Governor Kundi said the provincial government’s priority was to restore peace and strengthen the police force, stressing that development would follow once security was ensured. He said the police were at the forefront of the war against terrorism and needed to be adequately equipped to carry out their responsibilities. “Until we strengthen and facilitate [the police], how will they fight using just one Kalashnikov and a few bullets?” Kundi asked. While the government had announced compensation packages for the families of police martyrs and was working on improving police salaries, it would also provide the force with weapons, ammunition and other resources, Kundi stressed during his speech. “We talk a lot about merged districts, but as far as I know, not a single police line has been created in our merged districts, our former Fata. Look at their police stations, check posts, and facilities,” Kundi highlighted, adding that the government had directed the chief secretary and additional chief secretary to prepare a comprehensive package in this regard. He said the plan also included solarising and equipping police facilities. The governor pointed out the “lack of political ownership” previously with regard to the war against terrorism in the province. “When something happened here, voices always came from the assemblies saying that this is ‘not our war’. We don’t own it,” Kundi said. He questioned what the families of martyrs would say when political leaders did not take ownership of the war. “For whom did the martyr make this sacrifice? Was it for this soil, this country, or was it made under a specific agenda?” he asserted. “If I have a gunman who is there for my protection, and I say that I don’t even own this gunman, how will he protect me?” Kundi asked rhetorically. According to the governor, not owning the war indicated a lack of coordination. Kundi referred to the security situation in parts of KP, adding that political leaders, including a former chief minister and JUI-F’s Maulana Fazlur Rehman, had acknowledged difficulties in moving freely in certain areas. “If intelligence-based operations do not take place and the police and security forces do not conduct operations, how will these problems be resolved?” he asked. Kundi said the current set-up’s stance was “clear” and that decisions and policies would be made in Islamabad rather than “Kabul, Kandahar or Jalalabad”. The governor alleged that Afghanistan was facilitating India and Israel in using its territory against Pakistan. He referred to reports of drones entering Pakistan, saying some had crossed the border but were intercepted by Pakistani forces. He then criticised the lack of response by the previous government to statements by Afghan ministers threatening to take over Peshawar. Kundi said Pakistan had repeatedly raised its concerns about Afghan soil being used to facilitate terrorism at international forums through the Foreign Office and the deputy prime minister and foreign minister, but Kabul had not budged an inch on addressing the issue. “It is very clear that whoever does not accept our state, Constitution and laws cannot be engaged in dialogue. Anyone who takes up arms against the state cannot be offered dialogue; they will be responded to accordingly,” Kundi asserted. During his speech, the governor stressed the importance of winning public trust, recalling that the province began its journey towards peace in 2008, when it was grappling with suicide bombings, target killings, kidnappings for ransom, among other problems. He said public support had been crucial to previous military operations and would remain essential to counterterrorism efforts. “You saw we cleared Swat; the world’s largest displacement occurred at that time, and we rehabilitated the people. People supported us for the operation.” Reiterating that the government had a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, Kundi said the fight against it remained its foremost priority, with development coming afterwards. “You can build roads, large underpasses and even turn the city into a garden, but what is the point if the people themselves are not safe?” he said. He stressed that people needed to be assured that their children could go to school, college and playgrounds and return safely, while family members could travel to work or conduct business without fear. The governor also called for greater engagement of the province’s large youth population through “positive activities”.

items.title: Guinée : Baowu Resources expose les avantages du projet Simandou
items.description: Selon un communiqué de Baowu Resources parvenu à notre rédaction, l’entreprise chinoise a publié, le 6 novembre à Shanghai, en marge de la neuvième Exposition internationale d’importation de Chine (CIIE), un rapport thématique ESG consacré à la durabilité du projet minier de Simandou, en Guinée. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence du ministre guinéen de l’Environnement et du Développement durable, Fassou Théa. Au cours de cette cérémonie, celui-ci a souligné que « le projet Simandou était aujourd'hui bien plus qu'un projet minier. Il marque une transformation historique pour l'économie guinéenne et offre une opportunité exceptionnelle de création d’emplois, de développement des infrastructures et d'amélioration des conditions de vie des populations guinéennes », rapporte le communiqué. Le président de Baowu Resources, Cao Zhifu, a pour sa part réaffirmé l’engagement de l’entreprise à accompagner les différentes parties prenantes. Il a déclaré que « Baowu Resources était disposé à travailler avec toutes les parties pour faire progresser le développement durable de Simandou de manière plus stable, plus concrète et plus ambitieuse », indique la même source. Présenté comme le premier document public ESG consacré à Simandou, le rapport expose une démarche fondée sur le partenariat, le progrès et la prospérité, associant développement minier, protection de l’environnement et renforcement des capacités locales. L’ambition affichée est de faire bénéficier les populations guinéennes et les partenaires du projet des retombées de son développement, précise le texte.

items.title: «Le médicament n’est pas un produit ordinaire» : le Gabon veut encadrer la vente en ligne
items.description: Médicaments falsifiés, escroqueries, vol de données bancaires : l’achat de médicaments sur Internet expose les patients à des risques que le Gabon veut encadrer par la loi. Le 6 novembre à Libreville, la ministre de la Santé, le Pr Elsa Nkana Ayo-Bivigou, a ouvert un atelier national de l’Agence nationale du médicament et des autres produits de santé (ANMAPS), chargé de recueillir des propositions devant servir de socle à un projet de loi. Les principaux acteurs des secteurs concernés et les officiels immortalisés à l’ouverture des travaux. © D.R. La ministre de la Santé, le Pr Elsa Nkana Ayo-Bivigou, a ouvert, le 6 novembre à Libreville, un atelier national consacré à la préparation d’un cadre réglementaire pour la vente en ligne des médicaments au Gabon. Organisée par l’Agence nationale du médicament et des autres produits de santé (ANMAPS), cette rencontre, rapportée par l’Agence gabonaise de presse (AGP), vise à doter le pays d’un dispositif juridique adapté à la commercialisation croissante des produits pharmaceutiques sur Internet. «Le médicament n’est pas un produit de consommation ordinaire» Réunissant les acteurs des secteurs concernés, les travaux entendaient recueillir des propositions devant servir de socle à un projet de loi encadrant la commercialisation des produits pharmaceutiques en ligne. À l’ouverture, la ministre a reconnu les opportunités du numérique, tout en alertant sur ses dérives potentielles. « Si cette évolution offre de nouvelles possibilités aux populations, elle renvoie également à des enjeux majeurs en matière de sécurité sanitaire », a-t-elle relevé. Le Pr Nkana Ayo-Bivigou a par ailleurs rappelé que « le médicament n’est pas un produit de consommation ordinaire ». En menant cette démarche, les autorités sanitaires du pays souhaitent garantir la qualité, la sécurité et l’efficacité du médicament, depuis sa fabrication jusqu’à sa dispensation. « Sa commercialisation ne saurait donc être soumise aux seules règles d’une consommation classique, au risque de compromettre la santé des populations », a averti la ministre de la Santé. Protéger les patients des plateformes non autorisées Pour sa part, le directeur général de l’ANMAPS, le Dr Ange Mibindzou Mouelet, a souligné que cet encadrement renforcera l’homologation, la surveillance du marché et la vigilance sanitaire, tout en contribuant à l’objectif d’atteindre le niveau de maturité 3 en matière de régulation pharmaceutique. Il s’agit, en effet, de prévenir la circulation de médicaments falsifiés, sous-dosés, toxiques ou dépourvus de principes actifs, mais aussi les escroqueries et le vol de données personnelles et bancaires. Face aux plateformes non autorisées, les populations sont ainsi appelées à vérifier l’agrément des pharmacies, notamment auprès de l’Ordre national des pharmaciens. L’ambition est d’accompagner l’innovation numérique sans sacrifier la sécurité des patients et de garantir un accès fiable aux produits de santé. items.title: Égalité femmes-hommes : près de 80 % des Gabonais pour, mais la pratique ne suit pas
items.description: Près de 80 % des Gabonais adhèrent à l’égalité entre femmes et hommes, mais la pratique ne suit pas : discriminations et harcèlement persistent au travail, et les femmes, jugées aussi légitimes que les hommes en politique, ont moins facilement accès aux ressources nécessaires au développement de leurs communautés. Tel est l’enseignement de l’enquête Afrobarometer Round 11, présentée le 6 novembre à Libreville. Un moment de la dissémination du 6 novembre. © GabonReview L’égalité entre les femmes et les hommes semble s’imposer dans les perceptions des Gabonais. C’est l’un des principaux enseignements de l’enquête Afrobarometer Round 11, dont la représentation gabonaise a dévoilé les résultats le 6 novembre à Libreville. Réseau panafricain indépendant et à but non lucratif, Afrobarometer entend faire de la voix des citoyens un instrument d’orientation des politiques publiques et des décisions de développement. Au Gabon, l’enquête a été mise en œuvre par le Centre d’études et de recherches en géosciences politiques et prospective (CERGEP) de l’Université Omar Bongo (UOB), auprès d’un échantillon nationalement représentatif de la population adulte. Instantané et photo de famille à l’issue de la dissémination, le 6 novembre. © GabonReview Les résultats dessinent une opinion plutôt favorable à l’égalité des genres. Près de 80 % des Gabonais y adhèrent, en matière de droits, d’opportunités et de participation à la vie politique. Sur le terrain professionnel, les citoyens soutiennent également l’intervention de la loi pour garantir l’égalité salariale. Mais cette adhésion ne suffit pas à faire disparaître les discriminations et le harcèlement continuant de marquer les environnements de travail. En politique, le contraste est tout aussi net. Les femmes sont largement considérées comme aussi légitimes que les hommes pour briguer des responsabilités électives. Toutefois, leur accès aux ressources nécessaires au développement de leurs communautés demeure plus difficile. À la recherche de l’équité Entre l’adhésion de principe et les pratiques, l’écart souligne les limites d’une égalité davantage affirmée dans les principes que garantie dans les pratiques. Pour Marthe Oyane Metogho, enseignante-chercheure au département de Littératures africaines de l’Université Omar Bongo, la notion même d’égalité mérite d’être interrogée à l’aune des réalités culturelles africaines. « Du point de vue culturel, nous ne recherchons pas l’égalité. Ce que l’on recherche, c’est l’équité. C’est-à-dire qu’on reconnaisse chacun à sa juste valeur », a-t-elle plaidé. Un acteur culturel a, pour sa part, invité les décideurs à tirer les enseignements de ces données, en soulevant une question de fond : « Est-ce que les lois des sociétés patriarcales s’adaptent aux réalités des communautés matriarcales ? » Du côté de la société civile, Amaria Princesse Apinda, représentante du Réseau femme lève-toi (ReFleT), voit dans cette adhésion populaire un motif d’espoir, mais aussi une invitation à accélérer les réformes. Elle relève un décalage entre les réalités du terrain et les textes en vigueur. « Il y a encore beaucoup à faire par rapport à l’effectivité de certains textes qui contribuent à cette égalité », estime-t-elle. « Bien heureusement nous pensons que la population gabonaise est ouverte à cette évolution et donc, on va continuer de travailler par rapport à ça », a-t-elle ajouté. items.title: PM Shehbaz, Nawaz discuss ‘matters of national importance’ as Sharifs gather at Lahore's Jati Umra
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif discussed matters of “national importance” with PML-N President Nawaz Sharif during a visit to the latter’s residence in Lahore’s Jati Umra on Sunday, state-run Radio Pakistan reported . The outlet reported that the two leaders held detailed discussions regarding the country’s political situation as well as “other matters of national importance”. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Nawaz’s daughter, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, were also present on the occasion. PM Shehbaz briefed the PML-N president on the law and order situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and on recent initiatives taken for the development and prosperity of the province, Radio Pakistan added. The Centre has imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP since Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism, and the new administrative setup led by Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has stressed that improving counterterrorism measures is its topmost priority. Both PM Shehbaz and his brother Nawaz have defended the decision to impose the emergency, with the premier saying the federal government had been “compel­led” to take the step over security conce­rns and the elder Sharif arguing that the intervention should have come much earlier. The premier also apprised Nawaz of “the ongoing economic reforms by the government, the challenges being faced and the measures being taken to address them”, the outlet said. The meeting also deliberated on ways to improve the national economy further, it added.

items.title: MIC : Guinée–Türkiye, l’agro-industrie et les investissements au cœur de la mission
items.description: Transformer les ressources en Guinée, développer les partenariats industriels et ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives commerciales : ces priorités ont guidé les échanges du Ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, Monsieur Aboubacar KOUROUMA, au cours de sa mission en Türkiye. Le mardi 3 novembre 2026, au cours du forum africain « Agriconnect », une rencontres avec les milieux d’affaires turcs, la délégation guinéenne a présenté les ambitions économiques du pays et exploré les possibilités de les traduire en projets concrets. Faire de la transformation agricole un moteur de croissance Consacré au partage d’expériences et à l’identification d’opportunités dans l’agriculture et la transformation agricole, le forum Agriconnect a réuni plusieurs délégations africaines, en présence notamment des ministres du Commerce de Türkiye et du Sénégal. À cette occasion, le Ministre Aboubacar KOUROUMA a mis en avant la dimension inclusive et panafricaine du Programme de développement socioéconomique durable et responsable Simandou 2040. Il a défendu une ambition : permettre à l’Afrique de prendre pleinement sa place dans les chaînes de valeur mondiales en développant ses propres capacités de production et de transformation. « L’Afrique tient dorénavant à transformer ses ressources sur place », a-t-il affirmé. Au-delà du potentiel minier guinéen, le Ministre a rappelé la volonté du Gouvernement de faire de l’agriculture un véritable moteur de l’économie. La valorisation des terres agricoles et le développement de la transformation locale constituent, à ce titre, des leviers pour créer davantage de valeur et d’emplois en Guinée. Renforcer les échanges avec les entreprises turques La délégation a ensuite rencontré des représentants du MÜSİAD, une organisation patronale turque réunissant notamment des entreprises industrielles et commerciales. Les discussions avec les investisseurs, issus entre autres des secteurs de la construction et du commerce, ont porté sur le renforcement des relations économiques entre les deux pays. Les parties ont réaffirmé leur volonté d’intensifier leurs efforts pour atteindre l’objectif commun de 500 millions de dollars d’échanges économiques et commerciaux. Avec Albayrak, avancer vers des projets concrets En fin de journée, le Ministre et sa délégation ont été reçus par Monsieur Ahmet Albayrak, Président du Conseil d’administration du groupe Albayrak. Après une présentation du parcours du groupe, les échanges ont permis de faire le point sur ses activités en Guinée et d’examiner ses perspectives de développement à court, moyen et long terme. Le Ministre a invité le groupe à renforcer sa participation à l’industrialisation du pays, particulièrement dans la transformation agricole. Les deux parties sont convenues de poursuivre rapidement les discussions afin de faire émerger des projets concrets, susceptibles d’être mis en œuvre dans les meilleurs délais et bénéfiques aux deux pays. items.title: Élus locaux : signer un acte d’état civil sans vérifier, c’est risquer la prison
items.description: Signer trop vite un acte d’état civil peut mener en prison. Voilà l’un des avertissements adressés aux élus locaux lors du séminaire du ministère de l’Intérieur à l’hôtel de ville de Libreville, clos le 7 novembre 2026. Durant plusieurs jours, les membres des bureaux des conseils municipaux et départementaux ont été formés aux exigences juridiques, administratives et financières de leurs fonctions, à l’heure de la Ve République. Le procureur du tribunal de première instance de Ntoum, Roger Darnel Nguema-Ondo lors de son intervention, le 7 novembre 2026. © D.R. La gestion des collectivités locales ne s’improvise pas. Les élus locaux sont désormais appelés à faire preuve de davantage de rigueur dans l’exercice de leurs responsabilités. C’est l’un des principaux enseignements du séminaire organisé par le ministère de l’Intérieur à l’intention des membres des bureaux des conseils municipaux et départementaux, achevé le 7 novembre 2026 à l’hôtel de ville de Libreville. Au cours de cette rencontre, plusieurs ateliers ont permis aux participants de mieux appréhender les exigences liées à leurs fonctions. Parmi les thèmes abordés figurait la gestion des actes d’état civil. Le procureur du tribunal de première instance de Ntoum, Roger Darnel Nguema-Ondo, a particulièrement insisté sur les risques juridiques liés à la signature de documents comportant des irrégularités. « Souvent, il peut arriver que lors de la déclaration d’un enfant, il y ait une erreur sur le nom. Il peut arriver que l’acte soit signé par une personne qui n’a pas de compétences. Il peut arriver qu’il y ait une erreur sur la nationalité ou encore sur le nom des parents », a-t-il expliqué, avant de rappeler qu’en pareille circonstance, « il y a une procédure qui peut être faite devant les tribunaux de première instance ». Ce rappel n’a pas laissé les participants indifférents. Car si les actes sont préparés par les agents municipaux et départementaux, la responsabilité de leur signature incombe aux élus habilités. D’où la nécessité d’une vigilance accrue. « Quand un agent d’état civil vient proposer un document à ta signature, si tu n’es pas vigilant, tout de suite, tu le signes, et c’est la prison parce que c’est ta signature qui est engagée et non pas l’agent d’état civil », a prévenu Elfox Mbina, premier adjoint au maire de Ntoum. Outiller les élus, préparer le financement local Pour Alain Fernand Eye Nze, président du conseil départemental du Komo-Kango, cette formation constitue un apport important pour les responsables locaux. « Nous partons de là, suffisamment outillés, vu la qualité des thèmes qui ont été abordés. L’objectif, c’est justement d’opérer des changements », a-t-il souligné. Au-delà des questions d’état civil, les échanges ont également porté sur le Fonds de péréquation des collectivités locales et ses implications dans le financement des administrations décentralisées. Selon Yongui Medoux, directeur général adjoint du Fonds, le dispositif est déjà en service. « D’ici à 2027, nous serons en mesure de leur donner l’ensemble des procédures de collaboration entre le Fonds de péréquation des collectivités locales et les collectivités locales elles-mêmes », a-t-il indiqué, précisant que cette perspective reste conditionnée par l’inscription, dans la loi de finances, de la dotation spéciale de développement des collectivités locales. Cette session de formation devrait ainsi ouvrir la voie à d’autres séminaires, davantage ciblés, afin de permettre aux élus locaux de maîtriser les outils juridiques, administratifs et financiers indispensables à leurs missions sous la Ve République. L’enjeu est désormais de transformer ces enseignements en réflexes de gestion, au service d’une gouvernance locale plus rigoureuse et plus efficace. items.title: Le Cercle Sénégal-Maroc d’amitié et de fraternité dévoile ses ambitions au khalife général des mourides
items.description: Le Cercle Sénégal-Maroc d’amitié et de fraternité (CESEMAF) poursuit ses efforts en faveur du rapprochement entre les deux peuples. Une délégation de l’organisation, conduite par son président, Amadou Kane, a été reçue, samedi 7 novembre, par le khalife général des mourides, Serigne Mountakha Mbacké à Touba . Cette audience a permis aux responsables de présenter leur plan d’action ainsi que leurs initiatives dans les domaines social et éducatif. Au cours des échanges, le président du CESEMAF a annoncé plusieurs projets destinés à soutenir les communautés des huit anciens villages de reclassement social. Parmi les initiatives envisagées figure la mise en place d’activités productives, notamment la création d’une unité de transformation des déchets plastiques dans l’un de ces villages, situé dans la région de Kolda. Le projet vise à valoriser ces déchets en produits commercialisables et à générer des revenus pour les populations locales, particulièrement les femmes. L’organisation a également fait part de sa volonté de contribuer à la réhabilitation de la Maison du Sénégal au Maroc, notamment à Fès. Cette résidence, dont l’état de dégradation a été signalé par des dignitaires religieux, devrait bénéficier d’un programme de restauration avec l’appui des partenaires du CESEMAF. Sur le volet éducatif, onze bourses d’études, dont une entière et dix demi-bourses, ont été mises à la disposition du guide religieux. Une démarche qui traduit l’engagement de l’organisation en faveur de la formation des jeunes. À l’issue de l’audience, la délégation a sollicité les prières de Serigne Mountakha Mbacké pour la consolidation des relations d’amitié et de fraternité entre le Sénégal et le Maroc. Le secrétaire général du CESEMAF, Lahlou Sidi Mouhamed, a, pour sa part, invité les jeunes à la vigilance face à certains médias étrangers qui, selon lui, diffusent des contenus susceptibles de fragiliser les relations entre les deux peuples. items.title: Hamza Zahoor’s unbeaten century guides Pakistan U-19 to thrilling win over India
items.description: Hamza Zahoor produced a match-winning unbeaten century as Pakistan Under-19 defeated arch-rivals India by three wickets in a thrilling Group ‘A’ encounter of the ACC Men’s Under-19 Asia Cup at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Muscat on Sunday. Chasing 209, Pakistan reached the target in 48.1 overs, finishing on 211 for seven, with Hamza holding his nerve under pressure to steer his side home. The wicket-keeper-batter remained unbeaten on 100 off 108 balls, striking 10 fours and three sixes, and was named Player of the Match. Pakistan’s chase, however, was far from straightforward as India’s bowlers made early inroads to reduce them to 61 for five. Hamza then joined Hasnain Abbas Dar, who contributed 38, to revive the innings with a crucial partnership. With wickets falling at the other end, Hamza showed remarkable composure, combining caution with timely aggression to keep Pakistan on course. He eventually guided the lower order across the finish line with 11 balls to spare, completing a memorable century in the process. Earlier, India, after electing to bat, were bowled out for 208 in 46.3 overs. Their innings got off to a disastrous start when captain and opener Lakshya Rajesh Raichandani was dismissed for a duck off the second ball. India slipped further to 22 for three, leaving their middle order under considerable pressure. Arjun Rajput then mounted a spirited recovery with an outstanding 107 off 85 deliveries, hitting 11 fours and five sixes. However, the right-hander received little support from the other end as Pakistan’s bowlers maintained pressure and regularly picked up wickets to restrict India to a modest total. Ali Raza, Rizwanullah and Niqab Shafiq shared the spoils with three wickets apiece, while Mohammad Sayyam claimed one. The victory takes Pakistan to the top of Group ‘A’ with four points from two matches, having registered back-to-back wins. India, meanwhile, have two points from as many games, with one victory and one defeat. Both teams have one group fixture remaining, with the top two sides advancing to the semi-finals.
