items.title: RETHINKING PAKISTAN’S AUTO POLICY
items.description: For one woman interviewed for the 2019 social assessment of Karachi’s planned Yellow Line Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), getting to her job destination meant walking 20 minutes to a road crossing, paying for a rickshaw and then paying again for a bus. Other women interviewed for the assessment relied on shared three-wheelers that waited to fill up with passengers before leaving. For some, the journey could take two hours each way. Monthly transport costs ranged from Rs3,000 to Rs6,000 in households where incomes of Rs20,000 to Rs30,000 were common. Fares can eat into an already modest wage. An unreliable connection can make a worker late. A second fare at each end of the journey can make studying at a college or a job across town too expensive a proposition to take up. The draft for Pakistan’s Auto Policy 2026-31 revolves around car prices, manufacturers and tariffs. Yet, most households in the country own no car and struggle with the daily cost of commuting. Mobility for work, education and healthcare remains restricted due to unavailability of affordable and safe public transportation choices. How can Pakistan’s auto policy serve the people at large and not just the top decile of households in the country? THE FAULT IN OUR DRAFTS In April, when petrol rose by more than Rs137 a litre, governments briefly treated the price of a bus ticket as a cost-of-living issue. Islamabad announced 30 days of free public transport. Punjab’s relief ran for 69 days, with authorities estimating that hundreds of thousands of passengers a day used the free services. The relief ended, but the daily cost of getting to work remained. Pakistan now has a chance to address some of that cost through its next auto policy. The draft Auto Policy 2026-31 has been okayed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but is still awaiting final approval as the Ministry of Industries and Production is set to forward the draft policy to the Ministry of Finance, which aims to share it with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for review. This policy would reportedly reduce tariffs, open a formal route for commercial used-car imports and expand the role of electric vehicles. These changes could give car buyers more choice. The draft also shapes how buses and two-wheelers are taxed, which vehicles get incentives and where the proceeds of a proposed automobile levy go. The problem, in my view, is that the debate remains organised around the vehicle and its producer. The household experiences it as a sequence of fares, waits and transfers. An auto policy cannot run provincial bus services, but it can reduce fleet costs and make public support conditional on affordable service. That connects industrial policy to the ability to earn a living. Those decisions should be judged by what they do for the journeys people make every day. For most Pakistani households, the price of a bus ride is a more immediate concern than the price of a new car. WHO’S BUYING THE ALTO? Pakistan’s assemblers sold 155,631 passenger cars in 2025-26. Including separately reported jeeps and pick-ups takes four-wheeler sales to about 206,000. Motorcycle and rickshaw sales totalled roughly 1.97 million. My analysis of the 2024-25 Household Integrated Economic Survey (HIES) shows how differently Pakistanis get around. About 6.6 percent of households own a car and 57 percent own a motorcycle. Roughly 41 percent own neither. Among the poorest fifth of urban households, nearly two-thirds have neither vehicle and only about one in a thousand own a car. Among the richest urban fifth, more than one in five own a car. A Suzuki Alto VXR lists at about Rs2.99 million. The survey puts average household income at Rs82,179 a month, so the Alto costs more than three years of total income, before a household pays for food, rent or anything else. One reported estimate puts the likely reduction in small-car prices under the Auto Policy draft at around nine percent over five years. Applied to the Alto, that would still leave it costing about 33 months of average household income. There is a case for bringing those prices down faster. In 2006-07, local assemblers sold 180,834 cars, whereas passenger car sales reached just 155,631 in 2025-26. The figures are imperfectly comparable because classifications have changed and SUVs have become a bigger part of the market. Still, Indus Motors estimates that the industry can assemble about 600,000 vehicles a year and uses roughly 30 percent of that capacity. New manufacturers have entered the market, but factories still have far more capacity than the market can absorb. The entry of more assemblers does not by itself resolve this. If each operates a small plant behind similar tariff protection, the market can acquire more brands without acquiring the scale or price competition consumers need. Lower duties on finished cars would strengthen the pressure to compete, but duties on imported components also matter. A sensible transition should expose producers to competition while allowing them to obtain inputs at competitive prices. For some smaller imported cars, one reported tariff schedule keeps customs duty at 50 percent for the first two years and then brings it down in stages to 15 percent by 2030-31. Bringing those cuts forward would put earlier pressure on local producers to compete on price and quality. If the government also wants to discourage fuel-hungry vehicles, it can tax size or fuel use directly. A cut in customs duty does not translate directly into an equal cut in the showroom price. Exchange rates, other taxes and producer margins impact what the buyer pays. I would judge success by actual prices and product quality, rather than the number of assembly licences issued. A tariff timetable that can repeatedly be deferred offers consumers little assurance. Although Pakistan’s local car manufacturing capacity has more than doubled since 2006, annual sales (as denoted by the blue line) across the years have remained at a stagnated level | Author’s analysis of data sourced from the PIDE and the Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association (Pama) AN ELECTRIC SOLUTION? The distribution of electric vehicle incentives deserves the same scrutiny. Some reported proposals for electric cars include a favourable sales tax rate and a financing ceiling of Rs10 million. If a 17 percentage-point tax preference (the difference between tax rates on electric vehicles as compared to on an internal combustion engine vehicle) is applied to an Rs8 million pre-tax car, the buyer’s tax advantage would be Rs1.36 million. That is roughly the value of 21 electric-motorcycle subsidies of Rs65,000 each under the Pakistan Accelerated Vehicle Electrification (PAVE) programme. The actual benefit would depend on how the tax is applied and what the government ultimately approves. The comparison shows how much support can go to a single purchase. Equivalent fiscal support does not mean equal benefits from different vehicles. A higher loan ceiling does little for someone without a down payment or an income that a lender will accept. Eligibility matters as much as the advertised concession. Electric cars can cut petrol use, especially for people who drive long distances. But a household that cannot finance any private vehicle needs a different kind of help. A bus fare can determine whether someone in that household works at all. Car ownership remains heavily concentrated among wealthier households, while most urban Pakistanis in the lower income brackets have no personal vehicle | Author’s analysis of HIES 2024-25 data THE HIDDEN COST OF BEING UNABLE TO TRAVEL The poorest fifth of Pakistani households spent 4.8 percent of their budgets on transport, compared with 6.7 percent for the richest fifth. In cities, the respective figures are 4.2 and 6.5 percent. If spending were the measure of need, the figures would suggest transport was a bigger problem for the rich. But consider: a household survey counts the fare someone paid. It has no fare to record when a worker walks to save money, a woman turns down a job she cannot reach safely or a student stays home because college is too far away. The poorest fifth also spends almost half its budget on food, compared with about 29 percent for the richest fifth. Once food and the estimated rental value of housing are set aside, transport takes up a more similar share of what remains. The estimated rent includes the value of living in an owner-occupied home, even though no rent changes hands. Removing it from the comparison does not create cash for a bus ticket — it changes the denominator. I read the low transport share as a reason to investigate journeys people cannot make. The expenditure survey alone cannot tell us how many jobs were declined or classes missed. My analysis puts transport spending for the poorest fifth at about Rs254 per person a month. At Rs20 a ride, that pays for six complete return trips. A World Bank benchmark used in urban transport affordability studies allows for roughly 60 one-way trips a month. Even if someone in the poorest fifth put their entire transport budget towards a bus, they would still be well short of a month’s travel to work or school. Among poor urban households with at least one earner and neither a car nor a motorcycle, the survey implies about Rs9 in reported in-city fares per earner per working day. People may forget small fares when asked to recall spending over a year. The figures also cannot separate journeys made on foot from those abandoned altogether. Project documents for Karachi’s Red Line BRT estimate that about 40 percent of trips in the city are made on foot or by bicycle. Some people choose to walk or cycle. For others, it may be the only way to avoid paying for several rides on a single journey. The cost is easier to see against a wage. My analysis of the survey puts median monthly earnings for an urban paid worker at about Rs32,000. At Rs80 each way over 26 working days, the commute costs Rs4,160, or 13 percent of pay. A combination of wagons and rickshaws costing Rs200 a day takes Rs5,200, or more than 16 percent of pay. At the household level, two earners, each paying Rs20 in both directions over 26 working days, would spend Rs2,080 a month. Against the roughly Rs40,146 monthly budget for the poorest urban households in my analysis, that is just over five percent. At Rs80, the same journeys cost Rs8,320, or about 21 percent. These comparisons use survey-period budgets and illustrative fares, not today’s measured burden. They show why a fare that looks modest per trip can be unaffordable when paid repeatedly. For women in paid urban work, reported median monthly earnings were about Rs10,000, partly reflecting fewer hours of paid work. A 26-day commute at Rs80 each way would take about 42 percent of that amount. This is an illustration, since a woman earning Rs10,000 may work fewer days. It shows what fares can do to the gains from taking on more work. Distance can also put education out of reach. In the survey, about 1.3 million girls and young women and 900,000 boys and young men aged five to 24 had never attended school and cited distance as the reason. Where there is a school to go to, a safe, affordable journey can remove one of the barriers to getting there. Motorcycle ownership only partly solves this problem. A single motorcycle cannot necessarily serve two earners travelling in different directions and children going to school. Nor can we assume that every household member can ride it. Therefore, counting households with a vehicle tells us less than knowing who can use it, when and for which journeys. The economics of commuting favours public transport, as demonstrated by this comparison across one month | Author’s analysis of data sourced from the World Bank, PIDE and HIES A BUS PEOPLE CAN RELY ON On Lahore’s Orange Line train, about 51 percent of reported journeys were for work and 33 percent for education. In Peshawar, a 2023 account citing TransPeshawar (a public company established by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to manage, operate and maintain the Zu Peshawar BRT system) put women at about 30 percent of passengers on the bus rapid transit system, up from an estimated two percent on earlier services. Other published accounts put the newer figure closer to 20 percent. The new system offered separate entrances and reserved areas, better lighting, station security and more predictable service. Research in Lahore by economists Robert Garlick, Erica Field and Kate Vyborny offers a closer look at how transport impacts decisions about work. Through a job-search platform, the researchers offered commuting services to women. The offer of women-only transport more than doubled job application rates, while mixed-gender transport produced little response. The study measured applications, not jobs secured. It shows how the commute can deter women before an employer has even seen their names. Even a new bus can be difficult to board. Writing in Eos earlier this year, Samina Hassan Laghari and Arif Hasan described Karachi’s electric buses with about 30 seats carrying 70 or 80 people, sometimes more than 100. Women told them they had given up work because of the journey. The city’s bus fleet was reported at 1,029, against an estimated requirement of 15,000. Building more corridors can help, but people have to reach them. A cheap fare on the main route can lose much of its value if a passenger has to pay for a rickshaw to get to it. A well-lit stop is of limited use to a child who has to cross a dangerous road to reach it. The World Health Organisation (WHO) estimates roughly 28,000 road deaths a year in Pakistan, with pedestrians accounting for a large share. Official reported totals are much lower. Both the walk to the bus and the ride itself belong in a transport plan. Reliability matters as much as the fare. A daily-wage worker who cannot tell whether a bus will arrive in five minutes or 45 has to leave early or risk losing a shift. Karachi’s Red Line has faced a much longer timetable than originally envisaged. While cities build major corridors, they also need buses running between neighbourhoods, regular departures and connections that people can use without building an hour’s uncertainty into the day. A dependable service also reduces the unpaid time a worker must allow for delays. Time savings belong in the economic appraisal, even when they produce no additional fare revenue. They should be measured through actual waiting and journey times, rather than assumed whenever a new bus or corridor is announced. THE COST OF THE COMMUTE To compare the choices, I modelled the same trip across five modes, with 30 kilometres covered a day, 26 days a month. For private vehicles, the calculation includes ownership and financing costs as well as fuel or electricity. For the bus passenger, it includes a low main fare and some travel to and from the route. Under these assumptions, monthly costs per commuter are roughly Rs1,900 for a bus, Rs4,900 for an electric motorcycle, Rs5,200 for wagons and rickshaws, Rs7,000 for a petrol motorcycle and Rs39,900 for a small petrol car. The bus estimate includes a Rs25 fare and feeder journeys. The model assumes petrol at Rs378 a litre, 15 percent vehicle financing and some sharing of private vehicles. These are modelled costs, not quoted monthly instalments. The bus figure is what the passenger pays after public support; it is not the full cost of providing the service. The difference matters for the country’s import bill as well as the commuter’s wallet. Pakistan spent about $16.9 billion on petroleum imports in fiscal year (FY)26, compared with roughly $2.1 billion on imported vehicle assembly kits. The totals cover different categories, but they give a sense of the scale of dependence on imported fuel. In the model, moving one million daily commuters from motorcycles into small petrol cars would add about Rs394 billion a year to household costs and roughly $440 million to imports, including fuel and vehicles. Electric motorcycles offer substantial savings where people already ride petrol bikes. In the model, each rupee of public support for electric motorcycles saves households more cash and generally saves more on imports than a rupee spent on buses. A bus reaches people a motorcycle subsidy cannot readily serve, including students, older passengers and households that cannot buy a vehicle. That makes a case for supporting both. The journey being replaced matters. A bus carrying former wagon passengers has a different effect on imports from one attracting motorists. An electric motorcycle replacing a petrol motorcycle is different from an additional vehicle bought for convenience. My calculations assume those substitutions — they are not a forecast that every subsidised purchase will deliver the same saving. I would assess the programmes against what riders actually stop using. There is a case for electric buses on routes where charging and electricity supply can support them. In an illustrative comparison, a diesel bus covering 80,000 kilometres a year uses about 18,000 litres of fuel. At the diesel price of Rs395.20 a litre, effective on November 3, that costs about Rs7.1 million. Meanwhile, an electric bus, using about 96,000 units of power at an assumed Rs39.70 per unit, would spend about Rs3.8 million on electricity. The roughly Rs3.3 million difference comes before maintenance, financing and battery costs. A city weighing the higher purchase price should count that annual saving and the reduced exposure to a diesel price spike. Battery replacements and charging equipment also belong in the calculation. High utilisation helps recover the higher purchase price only if charging arrangements allow buses to run the promised service. Electric buses eliminate exhaust at the roadside, but overall emissions also depend on electricity generation. A national pollution claim needs a separate estimate. Women and men pictured driving electric bikes in Lahore: electric motorcycles offer substantial savings where people already ride petrol bikes | White Star HOW MANY BUSES CAN A LEVY BUY? The Automotive Development Levy (ADL), proposed in the draft for the Auto Policy 2026-31, could raise around Rs232 billion over five years. Its reported uses include export rebates and industrial upgrading. The government should consider putting a share towards public transport and say which proposed uses it would scale back to do so. Spread evenly, the projected revenue comes to about Rs46 billion a year. In my model, an electric bus running around 70,000 kilometres a year with 800 passenger boardings a day needs about Rs21.5 million in annual public support if borrowing costs 18 percent. At 11 percent, the contribution falls by about Rs5.5 million, to roughly Rs16 million. At that lower cost, the entire annual levy could support close to 2,900 buses. Using only a share would pay for proportionately fewer. The levy still needs approval and the figures depend on what buses cost, how much operators collect in fares and how many people ride. The assumptions also deserve scrutiny before anyone commits public money. Eight hundred boardings are not 800 different people: a commuter travelling both ways boards twice. At Rs25 a ride and 312 operating days, 800 daily boardings produce Rs6.24 million in annual fare revenue. If boardings halve, that revenue falls by Rs3.12 million, while much of the cost of owning the fleet remains. The model also assumes non-fare revenue at 37 percent of fares, which requires testing against actual advertising receipts. The 11 percent financing rate is an assumption rather than a financing commitment. Any interest subsidy must be funded and a guarantee can leave the state liable if repayments fail. Supporting 15,000 buses on those terms would cost around Rs240 billion a year. That is a recurring public expense. Pakistani households already spend an estimated Rs2.37 trillion a year on transport, according to the household survey. The question for the government is how much of that spending on a better service could save households and which trips people could make if the fare came down or the bus turned up regularly. Household savings cannot simply be netted against the government’s subsidy bill. A lower fare partly shifts costs from passengers to taxpayers — it does not eliminate them. Nor is all of the Rs2.37 trillion available to finance urban buses. The economic case must rest on savings in fuel and time, safer journeys and better access to work, alongside a credible plan for meeting the recurring budget commitment. WHAT THE POLICY NEEDS The policy can start by reconsidering the reported two percent development levy on buses and reviewing duties on electric buses and charging equipment. It can give affordable electric motorcycles and rickshaws greater priority in vehicle incentives. And it can make bus funding conditional on the service that provincial authorities and operators deliver. Localisation targets also need care. A rule designed around a petrol engine can penalise an electric motorcycle because its battery is imported. I would reward the value actually created in Pakistan, with a transition that allows battery and component suppliers to develop. The aim should be competitive suppliers that can sell beyond one protected domestic market. For bus funding, that means setting routes, fares and safety standards, then paying operators for running the scheduled service and maintaining the fleet. Provinces would have to pay on time and operators would have to run the promised service. Passengers should be able to see how often buses ran, how long they waited, and how many services were cancelled. Cities should also track who uses the system and ask people which journeys they still cannot make. A contract can make those obligations enforceable. The province could retain fare revenue and pay an operator for service delivered, with deductions for missed trips and safety failures. That reduces the incentive to overcrowd buses but leaves the province carrying the risk of weak ridership. Payment reserves and dependable budget releases would be necessary — private finance does not remove that obligation. Depots and power connections must be ready when the fleet arrives. I would begin with routes where demand can be tested, publish the results and expand where the service earns continued support. I would also want a travel survey to test the arguments made here. If low reported spending chiefly reflects short, affordable journeys and incomplete recall, the case for suppressed travel (when individuals do not undertake trips or activities due to barriers or constraints) would weaken. If well-run buses attract few riders, routes and spending should be reconsidered. A policy should allow those findings to change where the next rupee goes. Pakistan can keep a tally of cars coming off assembly lines. Over the next five years, it should also count how many more people can get to a job, a classroom or a clinic without buying a vehicle. For a woman making that journey, it comes down to what happens after the 20-minute walk: how long she waits, whether there’s room to get on and how much of her pay she has left when she gets home. The writer is a macroeconomist and professor of practice at IBA, Karachi. He can be reached at ammar.habib@gmail.com Published in Dawn, EOS, November 8th, 2026

items.title: Siblings acquitted in blasphemy case after 20 years
items.description: • SC sets aside death sentences upheld by LHC • Observes findings on mental illness raise doubts about culpability ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Saturday acquitted two brothers in a blasphemy case under Section 295-C of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), setting aside their death sentences earlier upheld by the Lahore High Court (LHC) over a decade ago. A three-judge SC bench, headed by Chief Justice of Pakistan Yahya Afridi and comprising Justices Shakeel Ahmad and Ishtiaq Ibrahim, took up criminal appeals against the Sept 17, 2015 decision of the LHC. The brothers, Liaqat Ali and Umar Draz, have spent around 20 years behind bars. They were convicted by a sessions judge in Jhang on March 27, 2006. The trial court sentenced both brothers to death and imposed a fine of Rs500,000 each, with five years’ rigorous imprisonment in default. The high court dismissed their appeals and upheld the convictions. The main SC judgement was authored by Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim. Justice Shakeel Ahmad concurred with the order but also annexed an additional note. According to the complaint, Umar Draz had begun making explicit blasphemous statements, leading to a marital dispute between him and his wife that culminated in divorce on March 13, 2006. Draz explicitly affirmed in writing his conversion from Islam in the divorce papers. During the return of his former wife’s dowry articles, a written document auth­ored by co-appellant Liaqat Ali was recovered. It also contained blasphemous assertions. On March 18, 2006, when the complainant and witnesses confronted the brothers over the alleged blasphemous material, both appellants acknowledged and verified the contents of the documents and unequivocally declared their willingness to reiterate their assertions before any forum. Before the SC, their counsel confined his submissions to the plea of mental unsoundness, arguing that the appellants lacked the requisite mens rea (guilty mind) at the time of the alleged offence. The SC examined three psychiatric assessments. An initial three-member medical board at DHQ Hospital, Faisalabad, found both appellants mentally sound in 2007. However, an eight-member Board of Certification diagnosed them with “bipolar affective disorder with psychotic symptoms” in 2023. A nine-member Board of Certification in September 2025 concluded that both brothers were suffering from “bipolar disorder current episode manic”. It described the condition as a chronic illness that was most likely permanent in acute cases, with absent insight and an inability to understand their acts at the time. The SC observed that the unanimous opinions of specialised boards comprising senior professors of psychiatry carried greater weight than the earlier assessm­ent by a board with only one psychiatrist. It also noted that bipolar disorder was episodic and had a genetic component, and that both brothers had been independently diagnosed with the same condition. “The appellants have spent around 20 years behind bars. In the light of the opinion of medical board which raises doubts regarding the culpability of the appellants, the benefit of doubt cannot be withheld from the appellants,” the judgement said. While acquitting the appellants, the SC also expected the executive director of the Punjab Institute of Mental Health, Lahore, to ensure that their medical treatment was not discontinued. Additional note In his concurring note, Justice Ahmad agreed with the acquittal but cautioned that a psychiatric diagnosis alone did not satisfy the requirements of Section 84 of the PPC. The judge distinguished medical insanity from legal insanity, noting that the key question was whether, at the time of the offence, the accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. He argued that legal accountability had to be balanced with humanity, explaining that true justice also included mercy when the law recognised a person’s lack of mental capacity. The note said the medical reports, along with the surrounding circumstances, created reasonable doubt. It also referred to Islamic principles of legal capacity and responsibility. Published in Dawn, November 8th, 2026

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : quatre lutteurs sénégalais à l’assaut de nouvelles médailles
items.description: Après une journée faste, ponctuée par deux nouvelles médailles d’or, le Sénégal entend poursuivre sa moisson aux Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. Quatre jeunes athlètes sont attendus, ce dimanche 8 novembre, sur les tapis de lutte de plage, avec l’ambition d’enrichir le tableau des médailles du pays hôte. La dynamique est lancée et les jeunes Sénégalais comptent bien la maintenir. Après les performances remarquables enregistrées en lutte de plage, avec les sacres d’Élisabeth Diatta et de Maguette Diop, le Sénégal retourne à l’arène ce dimanche pour une nouvelle journée de compétition. Quatre représentants nationaux sont en lice pour tenter de décrocher de nouvelles médailles devant leur public. Chez les filles, Ndeye Khady Anna Diatta, 17 ans, défendra les couleurs nationales dans la catégorie des moins de 45 kg. Sa compatriote Mery Manga, également âgée de 17 ans, sera engagée chez les moins de 65 kg. Du côté masculin, Ibrahima Sarr, 16 ans, tentera de s'illustrer dans la catégorie des moins de 70 kg. Ablaye Diouf, 17 ans, complétera la délégation sénégalaise chez les moins de 90 kg.Après les premiers exploits de leurs compatriotes, ces quatre jeunes lutteurs ont désormais l'occasion de prolonger l'élan et de faire vibrer davantage le public sénégalais. A.N

items.title: La machine du nectar d’arts ( 2/2)
items.description: « Je suis le moins créatif de cette équipe, le moins intéressant. Je travaillais avec des gens dont je suis fan. Ce n’est pas l’œuvre de Xalil, mais d’une équipe. J’étais juste derrière pour arbitrer. À la fin, on s’est retrouvé avec cette œuvre collective qui nous ressemble et nous rassemble », introduit Xalil quand on lui demande de présenter son équipe, dont personne n’avait jusqu’ici jamais organisé ou assisté à des cérémonies de Jeux olympiques. Lire aussi: Le « Nandité » aux commandes d’une académie (1/2) D’abord le metteur en scène, Adama Diop. « Il est à lui seul une machine, ce mec », s’exclame Xalil, qui ne connaissait pas cet acteur du théâtre avant de le contacter. « J’ai fait mes recherches et suis tombé sur lui. Je ne cherchais pas forcément quelqu’un de fou, mais d’un génie qui en voulait et qui était prêt à s’engager. Et quand j’ai vu qu’il a implanté une école et entendu son discours de lancement, je me suis que c’est lui qu’il me faut. Il n’habite pas toute l’année Dakar, mais il était super chaud quand je l’ai appelé pour représenter l’Afrique », confie Xalil Cissé, à qui Adama Diop a proposé de travailler sur la symbolique du cercle. Le cercle qui renvoie au bol en Afrique, à la cour du roi, aux assemblées…, mais rejoignent aussi les cinq anneaux olympiques. Ensuite, il y a Marième Ngom, coordinatrice générale Hmc (habillage, maquillage, coiffure), qui jouit d’une solide expérience dans l’écosystème du cinéma et de la mode. Selon Xalil, c’était un vrai soulagement d’avoir une personne qui comprenait rapidement et savait où elle allait avant même d’emprunter le chemin. D’ailleurs, Xalil précise que, hormis Adama Diop qu’il ne connaissait pas, il connaissait tout le reste de l’équipe qui était des noms qui s’imposaient à lui au fil de l’écriture du projet. La certitude s’est encore mieux affirmée avec les designers qui ont géré les trois temps de la cérémonie. Maguette Gueye de la Penderie de Maam, Khadija Bâ de L’Artisane et Selly Raby Kane. « Pour ces trois femmes, je n’ai même pas cherché à négocier. Il me les fallait absolument dans l’équipe », sourit Xalil Cissé. Maguette Gueye a habillé le Temps 1 de la cérémonie avec La Penderie de Maam, concernant tout ce qui touche au patrimoine, le sens de grandir sur l’Afrique. Elle a réalisé tous les costumes de cet acte, que ce soient les lutteurs, le tambour-major, les danseurs, AlKebulan, etc. Pour le Temps 2, qui raconte aujourd’hui, Khadija Bâ L’Artisane s’en est occupée. Elle est porteuse d’un style particulier, très réfléchi, qui valse entre modernité et patrimoine. Elle est surtout un as du fait-main, et son œuvre donne à résolument visualiser l’image urbaine dans son évolution spatio-temporelle. Selly Raby Kane, qui a vêtu le Temps 3, est déjà notoire dans le monde. Pour sa folie créatrice, son approche futuriste, son génie à poser des éléments du décor qui n’existent encore pas. Une constellation de lumières Quand Xalil Cissé parle d’Ismaïla Talla alias Iss 814, le directeur musical, on sent encore les étoiles dans les yeux. Il est clairement fasciné. « Ce mec, je l’appelle juste pour lui dire que j’ai besoin d’un directeur musical dans le projet artistique. Aussitôt je termine mon propos, comme un vrai génie, Iss 814 me fait un nombre incalculable de propositions, me dit comment le son doit être travaillé, comment doit se soutenir le rythme, etc. Il est même allé, dans ce même entretien téléphonique, à dessiner une trame de la cérémonie. Je me suis dit que je tiens mon gars moi », dit Xalil dans un éclat de rire qui signifie amusement et admiration. Iss 814, d’après lui, estimait qu’il lui manquait que cette corde à accomplir et accordait plus d’attention à ce moment que les disques d’or qu’il a déjà gagnés. Cette estime réciproque n’a pas cependant empêché qu’ils se sont chamaillés le long du projet, car « Iss 814 est tellement talentueux et fou qu’il court plus que la vitesse requise ». Eux deux laissaient libre cours à leur folie au studio. « On s’amusait un peu. On se disait par exemple essayons Saalimtoo, et bim ! il réécrit le thème et compose un truc de dingue », se souvient Xalil. Ainsi ont-ils eu leur musique de toute la première partie. Ensuite, puisqu’il fallait assumer la musique sous la férule du patrimoine africain, ils sont allés chercher des artistes et pris de vrais instruments pour rejouer toute la musique composée par Iss 814. Ouais, il fallait que le sabar, le tama, et tutti quanti disent leurs droits. Ensuite, il y a Khady Kassé, la scénographe. C’est elle qui a réalisé tous les éléments de scénographie physique sur cette performance. Elle est arrivée un peu tard dans le projet, mais a su s’y coller parfaitement selon le directeur artistique. Khady Kassé a été la scénographe de la 15e édition de la Biennale de l’art africain contemporain de Dakar, qui entame sa 16e édition dans moins de deux semaines (19 novembre – 19 décembre). Xalil Cissé avait l’atout d’avoir travaillé sur l’ouverture du Stade Abdoulaye Wade. Il connaissait donc l’endroit et avait identifié son espace. Les équipes techniques, qui capitalisaient plein d’événements dans ce stade, avaient également une parfaite maîtrise de ses infrastructures, « ce qui permettait une avance considérable malgré les délais relativement courts qui nous étaient impartis ». Il y avait par ailleurs une déambulation à la fin, qui était tel un défilé de modes. C’était quelque peu l’idée, une idée réalisée par neuf stylistes. Ils ont pour noms Rashid, Donatela Crea, Niuku, Stef de Karda, Weuz Owens, Gelisa Georges, Radji Radji, Jeyna A et Carmena A. « Ce sont de jeunes créateurs qui sont venus prêter main-forte avec 50 tenues, pour la fin très impactante de ce temps, suivant la direction artistique », explique Xalil Cissé. Dakar dans le «Dakar 2026» L’idée de Dakar, dans son authentique actualité urbaine, est transparue dans la performance. D’abord, la figure d’Issa Ramangellisa Samb Joe Ouakam, incarnée par l’artiste Obree Daman (Omar Samb de son vrai nom, par ailleurs parent de Joe Ouakam). « Il était très heureux d’avoir ce rôle, parce qu’il est aussi de la famille de Joe Ouakam. Puis il l’a très bien portée. Vous avez vu la pipe, la tenue ? », s’extasie encore Xalil, qui raconte qu’Obree Daman s’est aussitôt mis dans l’idée du designer. Et que dire des scènes de vie de Dakar ? Au-delà du clin à « Madame Brouette » de Moussa Sène Absa, c’est tous ces « pousse-pousse » (chariots à café) qui font le décor de la capitale, les « forox caaya », le tohu-bohu urbain, l’encombrement du piéton, les commerces sauvages, les petits larcins et le « tek xel », etc. « Tout cela c’est la ville, c’est Dakar », dit Xalil Cissé. Après la cérémonie, au milieu des satisfactions, beaucoup de spectateurs ont relevé la « cacophonie de la fin », considérant que l’équipe artistique s’est relâchée au terme du spectacle. En vérité, cette scène est un vrai faux capharnaüm, selon le directeur artistique. « Vous voyez, tout était ordonné, maîtrisé et réglé comme sur du papier à musique. On voulait montrer qu’on peut très bien, que tous les Africains peuvent très bien faire. Mais nous péchons souvent dans la finition. Nous avons un problème pour bien terminer. C’est cette image que nous voulions poser. Dire aux gens voilà, nous avons parlé au monde, maintenant parlons franchement entre nous. Voilà notre propre turpitude. N’est-ce pas notre sentiment quand nous circulons dans Dakar ? », questionne Xalil Cissé. L’art du désordre dans l’ordre. La claque sur les Sénégalais. Pour leur dire que « Voilà vous » ! « L’art, c’est aussi peindre une société. Relever des trucs qui ne sont pas bien », répète Xalil. N’est-ce pas aussi là que l’entrée du jeune artiste VJ tonne toute sa pertinence. Lui qui, entre le désordre médiatique et politique, a frayé un chemin où l’a retrouvé toute une jeune génération sans crier gare. Voilà, l’image d’une jeunesse qui émerge, même dans l’incertitude et le chaos. Un cosmogramme qui fait sens et plaisir La cérémonie d’ouverture des Joj « Dakar 2026 » était grandiose. Ce, par la fluidité d’une réalisation ayant rassemblé plus d’un millier de talents. 25 artistes et solistes, 54 performers, 32 acteurs et comédiens, 628 danseurs, 373 figurants, deux maîtres de cérémonie (Oumy Ndour pour la partie francophone et Y Dee pour l’anglophone), avec un plateau presque paritaire (45% de femmes pour 55% d’hommes). Puis, il y a eu les artistes vedettes. « Le choix de Kiné Lam, parce que je pense qu’il n’y a personne pour porter cette voix mieux que cette dame. On pourrait en dire autant pour Baaba Maal, qui est une voix panafricaine », pense Xalil Cissé. Le choix des artistes s’est fait depuis l’écriture du projet. Le directeur artistique privilégiait les artistes avec une écriture visuelle, dont l’expression artistique fait défiler dans l’esprit du spectateur des images s’adressant directement à sa sensibilité. C’est un narratif pour le continent. Et il fallait des artistes qui incarnent cette idée de l’Afrique. L’entrée d’Obree Daman, Maah Keïta (bass) et Sona Jobarteh (kora) était une transition entre deux temps. Il fallait des artistes modernes, porteurs de symboles puissants pour offrir un spectacle qui ne devait juste ne pas être pour les oreilles. L’inclusion était un maître-mot. L’Afrique qui rejoint l’universel était un impératif. Sona Jobarteh était donc là, musicienne dont la kora conquiert les scènes du monde. Souleymane Faye, quoique considéré comme marginal, reste un artiste avec une voix collective et attachante à notre imaginaire. Que dire de Kya Loum, dont la déclamation de l’hymne national a même fait frémir les moins patriotes ? La lutte sénégalaise, le « lamb », a aussi été un marqueur majuscule. Ce sport de chez a exposé sa panoplie culturelle, au travers du « bàkk », geste chorégraphique d’auto-détermination qui permet au guerrier ou au lutteur de dire sa puissance et lancer vaillamment un défi. À côté, il y a eu la prestation du « simb », le « faux-lion », notre cirque local qui saisit l’imaginaire de tout urbain. Par Mamadou Oumar KAMARA

items.title: Waleed Mohammed: Using art to preserve Sudan’s collective memory
items.description: Sudanese visual artist Waleed Mohammed is seeking to document and reclaim the country’s collective memory through artworks inspired by historical photographs and family albums. Drawing on his personal experience of war, displacement and the dispersal of his family, he uses painting, diverse materials and multimedia from his studio in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, to explore the transformations in Sudanese lives since the outbreak of war in April 2023, as well as memories of the years before it. The beginnings Waleed Mohammed’s relationship with painting began in childhood, before he decided to study fine art and specialise in the discipline. He graduated in March, shortly before the outbreak of war, following a long period of study. However, the events unfolding in Sudan forced him to leave the country and continue his artistic career abroad. He moved to Nairobi, where he embarked on a new chapter in his creative journey. Old photographs and family albums have been among his most important sources of artistic inspiration. Since childhood, he has been fascinated by images documenting Sudan’s history and the details of its social life. This interest is reflected in his work, through which he seeks to reinterpret the country’s visual memory in contemporary artistic forms. The artist draws on the archives of Sudanese photographers, including Rashid Mahdi and Gadalla Gubara, alongside other photographic sources. He seeks to transform images from family albums into paintings, so that they become more than historical documents, acquiring new meanings relating to identity, history, and collective memory. The concept of post memory Waleed’s work in this area engages with the archive of Sudanese photography, from family albums to old studio portraits. He revisits these images through painting, treating the process as an act of retrieval in which individual memory intersects with the collective trauma left by war, displacement, and family separation. His approach resonates with the concept of post memory, developed by Marianne Hirsch in her research on the children of Holocaust survivors. The term describes the relationship of a later generation to a trauma it did not experience directly, but which is transmitted through photographs, stories, and silence. The concept explores how subsequent generations relate to traumatic experiences endured by those who came before them. They do not remember these experiences themselves, but encounter them through stories, images, and inherited behaviours. Imagination, projection, and creativity mediate this relationship rather than direct recollection. A striking duality of colour characterises Waleed’s work. Monochromatic grey bodies and faces evoke the fading and deterioration of photographs over time, set against richly saturated fields of colour, including deep indigo blue, crimson red and earthy yellow. Faces become erased or obscured areas. Sometimes they are covered with embroidered threads; at other times, their features dissolve into the haze of brushstrokes or disappear behind dark glasses. Erasure itself becomes a visual language, conveying the fragility of memory and the loss of loved ones. Different techniques coexist on the picture surface, including painting, embroidery, Arabic calligraphy, and deliberately exposed brushstrokes. The concept also carries a critical dimension. Expanding its application too widely risks emptying it of meaning, while generalising trauma can obscure the distinctive experiences, memories, and identities of those who witnessed it. In this context, Waleed Mohammed, who has himself experienced war and displacement, is not a distant inheritor of memory but a witness to it. His work therefore intersects with post memory approaches without belonging to the concept in its strictest sense. This distinction gives his artistic experience its particular character. Speaking to Radio Dabanga from his studio in Nairobi, Waleed says his artistic experience cannot be separated from that of society, and that people’s suffering and the transformations they are experiencing have become central subjects in his work. Notable paintings The war and the dispersal of his family have had a profound influence on the subjects Waleed Mohammed explores in his art. He has become increasingly interested in individual and family photographs, seeing them as a means of maintaining his connection with relatives who have been scattered across different locations, including Libya. His painting Awab illustrates this aspect of his experience. It is named after his nephew, who is currently in Libya. In his interview with Radio Dabanga, Waleed explains that he chose his nephew’s name to express how much he misses him and his desire to preserve his presence through the artwork, despite the distances imposed by the war. Through this deeply personal experience, the artist seeks to express a much wider reality shared by Sudanese people separated by the conflict, forced to leave their homes and seek new lives in different places. Spaces of escape A striking painting of a woman hangs on the wall; her face covered with cotton fabric. Waleed later explains that it belongs to a collection of works he produced in Nairobi after the outbreak of war. Another painting from the same collection depicts a seated woman. He calls the series Spaces of Escape, drawing inspiration from the waves of displacement, forced migration and fragmentation that Sudan has experienced. Cotton features in some of the works, as part of his attempts to experiment with new locally available materials. The collection also makes extensive use of open spaces and empty areas, with figures depicted with incomplete features or partially obscured faces. According to Waleed, this artistic treatment reflects the disruption the war has brought to people’s lives and social relationships, forcing them to abandon familiar places and seek new spaces. Leaving home is no longer simply an escape from war, he suggests, but has become an attempt to build a different life in the places where displaced people have arrived. A painting of the mother of the artist Waleed Muhammad ‘Something special’ In one corner of the exhibition hangs a particularly significant painting of Waleed’s mother. He describes it as one of the works that inspires him and gives him a sense of closeness to her. It holds a special place in his heart. He painted it last year in the Ugandan capital, Kampala. Another work, entitled Something Special, is based on a photograph by Rashid Mahdi. Waleed explains that the painting dates back to 2022, when he produced it for a group touring exhibition that travelled to several European cities. It was one of three paintings he contributed to the exhibition, and the original photograph particularly caught his attention. The artistic approach, he says, reflects the disruption the war has brought to people’s lives and social relationships, forcing them to leave familiar places and seek new spaces. Leaving is no longer merely an escape from conflict, but an attempt to build a different life in the places where displaced people have found themselves. Incomplete images and the recovery of memory Waleed Mohammed’s interest in memory extends to the use of a variety of artistic techniques, including multimedia and a process known as photocopy transfer. This technique allows photographs to be transferred onto a painting surface, where the artist can then work on them by hand using different materials. In several of these works, the photographs appear incomplete, with sections missing or areas left blank. This is deliberate, encouraging viewers to reflect on what has disappeared and what the image can no longer fully reveal. The idea intersects with his use of cotton, which can conceal certain features or make them less distinct, opening up space for reflection on absence, memory, and fragmentation. Since the outbreak of war, the artist has returned more frequently to his family archive, alongside the historical photographs that inspired his earlier work. Personal photographs have become a means of reconnecting with family members while also expressing the collective memory of Sudanese people through everyday details and individual experiences. Some of his paintings depicting children also carry memories of the early stages of his artistic journey. He drew inspiration from old photographs and archival material, including images and references associated with Khartoum magazine. These works formed part of his first solo exhibition, which he held in Khartoum. The painting ‘Survivors’ Among the works associated with that period is a painting entitled Survivors. After the exhibition ended, the painting was taken to Germany, before Waleed recovered it several months ago. He recalls his former studio in Khartoum as an important milestone in his artistic career. Returning to the city after the outbreak of war, he found that the studio was still standing and that many of his paintings and other works had not been stolen. The survival of these works gave him a sense that part of his memory and artistic experience had been preserved, despite the destruction Sudan has suffered and the loss and dispersal experienced by its people. Art as a space for expressing collective experience In his interview with Radio Dabanga, Waleed Mohammed says his personal experience of displacement has had a direct impact on his work. An artist, he believes, carries within them part of their community’s experience and cannot genuinely express people’s suffering without engaging with it. As a result, the subjects he explores are closely connected to both his personal experiences and the challenges facing Sudanese people amid the war. He says his artistic perspective changed after leaving Sudan and moving to Nairobi. The experiences and events people go through influence how they think and the subjects they choose to explore. For Waleed, the artistic message remains open to development as circumstances change and life raises new questions about memory and the future. International events and exhibitions Despite the circumstances imposed by the war, Waleed has continued to participate in artistic events outside Sudan, including exhibitions and programmes in Kampala, Europe, and the United States. He has also held a solo exhibition in Kampala and taken part in artist residency programmes, which have given him access to studio facilities and opportunities to engage with artists from different backgrounds. He is currently preparing for further exhibitions and artistic events during the coming year, as he seeks to continue developing his career despite the challenges of displacement. ‘Shilla’: bringing Sudanese artists together in Nairobi Together with other Sudanese artists, Waleed Mohammed established an art collective in Nairobi called Shilla, following discussions about the importance of collaboration among artists who have been scattered across different countries by the war. The group aims to move beyond the isolation of individual artistic experiences and create a shared space for working, creating, and expressing issues affecting Sudan through art. It has already held two exhibitions in Nairobi, and its members hope to demonstrate the ability of Sudanese artists to continue creating despite the circumstances of war and displacement. The collective also seeks to raise public awareness of what is happening in Sudan and introduce audiences to the experiences of Sudanese artists. An international award This November, Waleed is preparing to receive an award from the Prince Claus Fund, a Dutch organisation based in Amsterdam which recognises 100 artists from around the world each year. In his interview with Radio Dabanga, Waleed expresses his happiness at being announced as one of the 100 artists selected internationally for the award. However, he also acknowledges mixed feelings about personal achievements being celebrated against the backdrop of the difficult circumstances facing Sudan and its people as a result of the war. The award announcement coincides with the organisation’s celebration of its 30th anniversary this month. A message to the Sudanese people In his message to the Sudanese people, Waleed Mohammed emphasises the importance of dialogue and working together to resolve disagreements. Sudan, he says, is a country that belongs to everyone, and addressing its problems requires people to sit together and engage in dialogue before it is too late. items.title: MIC: Guinée–Türkiye, l’agro-industrie et les investissements au cœur de la mission
items.description: Transformer les ressources en Guinée, développer les partenariats industriels et ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives commerciales : ces priorités ont guidé les échanges du Ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, Monsieur Aboubacar KOUROUMA, au cours de sa mission en Türkiye. Le mardi 3 novembre 2026, au cours du forum africain « Agriconnect », une rencontres avec les milieux d’affaires turcs, la délégation guinéenne a présenté les ambitions économiques du pays et exploré les possibilités de les traduire en projets concrets. Faire de la transformation agricole un moteur de croissance Consacré au partage d’expériences et à l’identification d’opportunités dans l’agriculture et la transformation agricole, le forum Agriconnect a réuni plusieurs délégations africaines, en présence notamment des ministres du Commerce de Türkiye et du Sénégal. À cette occasion, le Ministre Aboubacar KOUROUMA a mis en avant la dimension inclusive et panafricaine du Programme de développement socioéconomique durable et responsable Simandou 2040. Il a défendu une ambition : permettre à l’Afrique de prendre pleinement sa place dans les chaînes de valeur mondiales en développant ses propres capacités de production et de transformation. « L’Afrique tient dorénavant à transformer ses ressources sur place », a-t-il affirmé. Au-delà du potentiel minier guinéen, le Ministre a rappelé la volonté du Gouvernement de faire de l’agriculture un véritable moteur de l’économie. La valorisation des terres agricoles et le développement de la transformation locale constituent, à ce titre, des leviers pour créer davantage de valeur et d’emplois en Guinée. Renforcer les échanges avec les entreprises turques La délégation a ensuite rencontré des représentants du MÜSİAD, une organisation patronale turque réunissant notamment des entreprises industrielles et commerciales. Les discussions avec les investisseurs, issus entre autres des secteurs de la construction et du commerce, ont porté sur le renforcement des relations économiques entre les deux pays. Les parties ont réaffirmé leur volonté d’intensifier leurs efforts pour atteindre l’objectif commun de 500 millions de dollars d’échanges économiques et commerciaux. Avec Albayrak, avancer vers des projets concrets En fin de journée, le Ministre et sa délégation ont été reçus par Monsieur Ahmet Albayrak, Président du Conseil d’administration du groupe Albayrak. Après une présentation du parcours du groupe, les échanges ont permis de faire le point sur ses activités en Guinée et d’examiner ses perspectives de développement à court, moyen et long terme. Le Ministre a invité le groupe à renforcer sa participation à l’industrialisation du pays, particulièrement dans la transformation agricole. Les deux parties sont convenues de poursuivre rapidement les discussions afin de faire émerger des projets concrets, susceptibles d’être mis en œuvre dans les meilleurs délais et bénéfiques aux deux pays.

items.title: Le « Nandité » aux commandes d’une académie (1/2)
items.description: Il était d’abord un visage bien connu de l’écosystème des industries culturelles et créatives, pour en être l’un des plus grands ambassadeurs, avant de dévoiler le grand artiste qu’il est au monde, au gré de la cérémonie d’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse « Dakar 2026 ». Directeur artistique des cérémonies de cet événement olympique mondial, Ibrahima Cissé dit Xalil a, avec son équipe, ébloui le monde par une performance d’ores et déjà dans les annales. Avec des arts éloquemment mâtinés des authenticités de notre patrimoine. Chez Ibrahima Cissé dit « Xalil », la création part des fragments de nos imaginaires. Sa pratique rencontre ensuite leurs sens. Il replace ces débris, porteurs de couleurs insoupçonnées de nos patrimoines et identités, pour construire une fresque où chacun de nous trouve inévitablement sa part. C’est la même recette, « qui n’a rien de miraculeux », que Xalil Cissé a reconduite à l’échelle africaine, en tant que directeur artistique pour la cérémonie d’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse « Dakar 2026 ». Oui, « L’Afrique accueille, Dakar célèbre ». Pour Xalil, « Boy Dakar » abouti de son état, il fallait donner corps à ce slogan, partant de ses propres considérations artistiques. Il l’a dit lui-même, au terme du spectacle, dans une réaction devenue culte, « C’est l’Afrique qui est ainsi riche, on n’a pas besoin d’alchimie ». Ainsi donc, pour Xalil Cissé, toute la performance n’était qu’évidences et articulations (maîtrisée, bien sûr). L’évidence d’une mémoire commune de l’Afrique qu’il restait à sublimer, par le génie collectif d’une équipe sénégalaise d’exception qui avait l’authenticité comme ligne directrice. Lire aussi: La machine du nectar d’arts ( 2/2) Nous avons trouvé Ibrahima Cissé dit Xalil, directeur artistique des cérémonies des Joj « Dakar 2026 », jeudi soir à Kër Ayo (siège Cojoj) à Ouakam. Décontracté dans son pantacourt noir de même couleur que son t-shirt agrémenté d’une broche de L’Artisane, chaussettes dépareillées rouge et mauve, Xalil est déjà tourné vers l’organisation de la cérémonie de clôture. Quand nous lui demandons l’esprit qui a présidé à la conception de la trame de la cérémonie d’ouverture des Joj « Dakar 2026 », le samedi 31 octobre, la réponse sonne simple. « Le projet est parti, de base, sur l’idée de la famille. La trame est articulée autour de ça. « Maam, Doom, Sët » (grand-mère, enfant, petit-fils), tout est parti de là », nous confie Xalil, qui explique que le défi suivant était de mettre cette famille dans un plan plus global qui a « l’Afrique au cœur et l’universel comme but ». C’est ainsi qu’il commençait à se questionner sur comment s’adresser au monde avec notre patrimoine, et aller à contre-sens des diktats du digital et des logiques occidentales. « C’est là que nous avons fouillé dans la tradition, pour parler transmission et trouver cette proposition africaine assumée. Dès le départ, j’avais exclu une fixation sur la technologie, car il ne me fallait surtout pas perdre de vue la centralité de l’humain », confesse le directeur artistique des cérémonies des Joj « Dakar 2026 » (cérémonies d’ouverture et de clôture, les 153 de remise des médailles). Son premier chantier était d’identifier tous les arts dont il aurait besoin (arts vivants, cinéma, design, musique, etc.). S’adresser au monde par notre patrimoine Comment intégrer le cinéma, par exemple, s’était demandé Xalil. En ramenant ces symboles usurpés, s’est répondu Xalil, tels que la moto à cornes dans « Touki Bouki » de Mambety, que Beyonce et Jay Z avaient subtilement prise à leur compte. Oui, la performance du samedi 31 octobre signifiait aussi résistance, à l’heure où l’Afrique réclame ses récits ! Encore sur les symboles, AlKebulan portait les mêmes chaussures en or que Linguère Ramatu dans « Hyènes ». C’est le retour de la Femme pour reprendre ses droits et sa prééminence dans l’échelle de l’humanité par le sceau de la maternité. « Maintenant, il nous fallait mettre tout cela dans une idée non d’opulence mais de richesse simplement, dans les éléments de composition qui nous définissent », souligne Xalil, pour qui il ne fallait juste pas bâtir sur une Histoire autre que celle de l’Afrique. On a vu la figure de Cheikh Anta Diop, convoqué avec son laboratoire Carbone 14, selon Xalil, pour montrer que l’Afrique n’a pas que le rythme et l’entrain à offrir. « Nous avons des scientifiques, des intellectuels qui ont atteint les plus hauts sommets de la recherche. Nous n’avons à pâlir devant aucun nom… », martèle Xalil. D’ailleurs, l’évocation d’AlKebulan vient de là. C’était, au-delà d’un hommage, une réhabilitation populaire du « Professeur » Cheikh Anta Diop, au regard de sa contribution dans la reconnaissance du continent comme berceau de l’humanité et de l’homme noir dans toute sa dignité humaine. Même ce parti-pris ne saurait froisser Senghor d’outre-tombe, tant la manifestation culturelle de la créativité nègre a montré sa force dans cette performance. AlKebulan, Keb, Sitoé. La science, la culture et nous. Pour la référence à AlKebulan, Xalil est encore parti des écrits des idées de Cheikh Anta Diop, quoique des voix dissonantes réfutent la thèse. Selon l’historien sénégalais, Alkebuland (interprétée par Nicole Marignale) est l’ancien nom de l’Afrique, signifiant « Mère de l’humanité ». Cette figure métaphorique de la mère, forte, belle et résiliente a lancé cette cérémonie sous le sceau de la transmission. Sitoé (Sitoé enfant avec Sally Diène, et Sitoé adulte avec Oumy Ndong) est un prénom local et un hommage à la Sénégalaise, à sa résistance en référence à l’héroïne casamançaise Aline Sitoé Diatta. Elle représente l’Afrique du futur, enracinée dans ses traditions et tournée vers l’avenir. « Voilà pourquoi elle a reçu les transmissions, par le symbole de la kola et le flambeau, pour perpétuer le legs », déchiffre Xalil. Keb (Keb adulte avec Malang Sonko et Keb enfant avec Elijah Fall), nom d’origine égyptienne, est historiquement associée à la connexion entre l’humanité et la terre. C’est la représentation de l’Afrique d’aujourd’hui, avec une jeunesse vibrante, inventive et visionnaire. Par Mamadou Oumar KAMARA

items.title: Sénégal : 21 morts dans le naufrage d’une pirogue de migrants
items.description: Au moins vingt-et-une personnes sont mortes dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants au large de Kébémer, dans le nord-ouest du Sénégal, ont indiqué samedi soir les autorités. « Au soir du 7 novembre 2026, le bilan provisoire fait état de 21 corps sans vie et d'un rescapé », a indiqué le ministère sénégalais de l'Intérieur dans un communiqué, qui ne précise pas le jour du drame. « Les services compétents de l'État sont mobilisés pour poursuivre les recherches, porter secours aux éventuels rescapés et accompagner les familles », a-t-il ajouté. Des milliers de personnes originaires d'Afrique de l'Ouest, en majorité des jeunes, tentent depuis des années de gagner clandestinement l'Europe en empruntant la route de l'Atlantique, principalement vers l'archipel espagnol des Canaries, à bord d’embarcations surchargées, souvent vétustes. Selon le quotidien national Le Soleil, le naufrage s'est produit au large des côtes de la localité de Loumpoul, dans la région de Louga (département de Kébémer), entre Dakar et Saint-Louis. « La plupart des victimes seraient originaires des communes de Léona et de Thiéppe », dans le même département, ajoute le quotidien. Samedi également, la gendarmerie sénégalaise a annoncé avoir intercepté au large de Dakar 142 migrants clandestins, dont plusieurs femmes et des enfants, qui tentaient de rejoindre l'Espagne à bord d'une pirogue. Des milliers de personnes sont mortes ou ont disparu en tentant de rejoindre ainsi l'Europe ces dernières années. items.title: Broken record: Pakistan struggles with refugee influx; US supports Iran against the Soviet Union
items.description: As Pakistan took its first few steps, the massive logistical task of accommodating millions of refugees in the midst of widespread communal violence was a major challenge for the state. The issues of Sept 8-14, 1947, documented these difficult times. In happier news, the Urdu Anjuman met for the first time in Karachi, while in a strange twist of history, the US came to Iran’s defence in the face of Soviet threats. The great migration The partition of the subcontinent had resulted in one of the largest — and bloodiest — mass migrations in human history. In the second week of September, the pages of Dawn documented the massive flow of refugees in both directions as communal violence continued, while the newborn state struggled to protect, house and feed millions of people. In the Sept 8 issue, Mr Sri Prakasa, the Indian High Commissioner in Pakistan, was quoted as saying that “at present, nearly 300,000 people must be on the move from Pakistan to India and vice-versa and it was estimated that about 1,000,000 persons had already changed sides in both directions”. The refugees coming from India were mainly headed to Karachi, then the federal capital, and Punjab. In the Sept 10 issue, it was noted that “refugees from Hindustan are pouring into Karachi in ever increasing numbers.” However, the outflow in the other direction was equally considerable. In a related report, it was mentioned that “the mad rush of evacuees from Karachi is reaching its zenith. The police had to disperse several times crowds which had assembled at the office of the Bombay Steam Navigation Company to get passages to Hindustan”. The influx into Punjab was no less intense. In the Sept 11 issue, a report documented that “the total number of Muslim refugees which have arrived from the East Punjab into the West Punjab up-to-date has reached the huge figure of 12 lakhs and almost one half of this number has already been absorbed into the economic life of this province. …” Food scarcity The huge influx of people was amongst the reasons for shortage of food in the early weeks of Pakistan’s existence. As a headline in the Sept 8 issued noted, ‘Pakistan food situation becoming very acute’. Other factors behind the scarcity were export to India — now another country — as well as floods. But as the report put it, the “refugee problem coupled with the ‘scorched-earth’ policy carried out by some evacuees from the West Punjab — destruction of foodgrains, livestock and agricultural implements — have put an enormous strain on the food and administrative resources of the West Punjab.” Though those were exceptionally tough times, as the young state had to arrange food for a large population in war-like conditions, today, decades after the establishment of Pakistan, a much more experienced state is still unable to properly feed its people, particularly children. Millions of children suffering from stunting and wasting due to malnutrition point to this depressing reality. Delhi in flames While there was communal violence across the subcontinent in the run-up to Independence and the weeks and months thereafter, in the week under review, New Delhi, the Indian capital, experienced particularly brutal violence. ‘Delhi in flames’ the banner headline in the Sept 9 issue read. “Delhi is in flames. The administration has completely broken down. The troops seem out of control”, the report said, detailing a nightmare scenario. “Monday [Sept 8] was indescribably terrible throughout Delhi and New Delhi. It is impossible to say how many were killed on Sunday and Monday. That there has been extensive butchery everywhere is admitted by official quarters”. Freedom was supposed to be a moment of joy; the end of nearly a century of foreign bondage. But as these horrific accounts illustrate, that joy would be short-lived, as savagery was unleashed. Those who witnessed with their own eyes this madness have nearly all met their Maker, or are in the twilight of their lives. Yet the wounds of that period have yet to heal, as the continuing toxicity marking relations between Pakistan and India shows. Urdu Anjuman formed Though many amongst the elite pay only lip service to Urdu, the national language is key to preserving the culture and civilisation of the subcontinent’s Muslims. That’s not to take anything away from other languages spoken in Pakistan, which are all important and deserve respect and support. But Urdu and Pakistan are joined at the hip, and as the issue of Sept 9 noted, the formation of the Urdu Anjuman was a major event in the nation’s cultural history. The initial meeting was held in Karachi’s YMCA Hall on Sept 8 “under the Presidentship of Pir Illahi Bakhsh”, Sind’s education minister. “The organisation will serve as a nucleus for the propagation of Urdu throughout Pakistan,” the report said. In a message, Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan said: “It is fitting that Karachi should be the centre of the Urdu Anjuman-Pakistan. … Urdu has been a safe custodian of our cultural heritage and has formed an international link.” US support for Iran The truth can sometimes really be stranger than fiction. Today the US and Israel are locked in battle with Iran, and chances of fresh aggression against the Islamic Republic remain. However, in 1947, as the Iranians, then ruled by Mohammad Reza Shah, who was deposed by 1979’s Islamic Revolution, experienced tensions in their relations with the Soviet Union, guess who (rhetorically) came to Tehran’s defence: the US. As mentioned in the Sept 12 issue, the Iranians had reportedly repudiated the Soviet-Iran oil agreement, which didn’t go down well in Moscow. The kerfuffle caused the American ambassador in what was then called Teheran to make an impassioned plea for Iranian sovereignty. Of course we all know how, over the decades, the US has meticulously respected the sovereignty of states, and refused to meddle in their internal affairs (wink, wink). Mr George Allen, the US Ambassador in Teheran, was quoted as saying that “Iran’s resources belong to Iran. Iran can give them away free of charge or refuse to dispose them at any price. … Iranians may rest assured that the United States people will support fully their freedom to make their own choice.” You can’t make this stuff up. With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it. Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

items.title: Djulasso/Lélouma : ces magnifiques cascades qui vous fascinent de loin à Balaya
items.description: Majeusteuses, sauvages et presque inaccessibles, Djulasso s’admirent et fascinent de loin. Elles sont situées à Koura Tiwdé un district relevant de la sous-préfecture de Balaya à Lélouma en moyenne Guinée. À environ une trentaine de minutes de marche sur la partie située à droite du village de Thiéwéré, se dévoile, depuis le sommet d’une montagne ces impressionnantes cascades. (…). Le bruit des cascades s’entend aussi de très loin. Nichées dans un paysage très montagneux, ces chutes d’eau vous livrent un spectacle naturel fascinant. Sur plusieurs dizaines de mètres de hauteur, l’eau jaillit par pallier et se jette dans le vide avec une impressionnante force. Dans les alentours, des gigantesques montagnes se dressent comme pour garder et y veiller jalousement à ces cascades. En contrebas, une forêt verdoyante se dévoile. Ici, l’eau, la roche et les montagnes composent un paysage grandiose et avec une scène qu’on contemple davantage qu’on ne l’explore. Là, la nature a imposé ses propres limites. Les montagnes quant à elles, imposent le respect. Ces cascades sont là. Elles sont très visibles mais presque hors de portée. C’est comme un patrimoine naturel qui garde jalousement une part de son mystère. C’est ça aussi qui rend ces cascades très particulières.

items.title: Guinée : Tout savoir sur les élections régionales (sièges à pourvoir, électeurs concernés, mode de scrutin, etc)
items.description: Prévues pour le dimanche 29 novembre 2026, les élections régionales s'annoncent comme un tournant majeur pour la gouvernance locale en Guinée. La Direction générale des élections a détaillé les modalités de ce scrutin indirect, ainsi que la répartition précise des 424 sièges à pourvoir à travers le pays. ​Comment va se dérouler le vote ? ​Le mode de scrutin retenu est le vote indirect. Cela signifie que ce ne sont pas les citoyens directement dans les urnes qui élisent les conseillers régionaux, mais bien leurs représentants locaux. ​En pratique, les conseillers communaux élisent les conseillers régionaux parmi leurs propres membres selon un barème de représentation bien défini : ​Un conseil communal comptant entre 11 et 29 membres élit 1 représentant. ​Un conseil communal de plus de 29 membres en élit 2. ​Le scrutin se déroulera sous un format majoritaire à un tour. Les vainqueurs obtiendront un mandat de 5 ans, qui pourra être renouvelé. ​Répartition des 424 sièges par région ​Le nombre de conseillers régionaux attribué à chaque région dépend directement du nombre de communes qu'elle représente. L'arrêté de mars dernier fixe le volume global à 424 sièges, répartis ainsi : Région et Nombre de conseillers régionaux à pourvoir Kankan : 83 sièges Nzérékoré : 76 sièges Labé : 56 sièges Kindia : 55 sièges Faranah : 50 sièges Boké : 42 sièges Mamou : 38 sièges Précisions institutionnelles importantes ​La Direction générale des élections a tenu à apporter une nuance technique concernant l'évolution récente du territoire : les localités de Siguiri et Beyla ont bien été érigées en régions administratives le 20 août 2026. ​Toutefois, ces deux entités ne disposent pas encore du statut de collectivités décentralisées — une transition qui nécessite l'adoption d'une loi. Par conséquent, les chiffres communiqués pour ce scrutin reposent sur l'arrêté de mars, qui est antérieur à leur création officielle en tant que collectivités.

items.title: Festival du court métrage Ouaga Côté Court 2026 : 55 films de 33 pays au programme du 14 au 21 novembre
items.description: La 5e édition du Festival international du court métrage Ouaga Côté Court (OCC) se tiendra du 14 au 21 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, sous le thème « Le cinéma qui rassemble ». En prélude à l'événement, le comité d'organisation a animé une conférence de presse le samedi 7 novembre 2026 afin de présenter la programmation et les ambitions de cette édition. Du 14 au 21 novembre 2026, Ouagadougou accueille la 5e édition du Festival international du court métrage Ouaga Côté Court. 55 films de 33 pays sont inscrits au programme. Selon la promotrice du festival, Irène Tassembédo, l'initiative répond à un déficit structurel de diffusion des courts métrages sur le continent africain. « On produit des films, on forme de jeunes cinéastes, on développe des talents extraordinaires, mais où peut-on voir leurs œuvres ? Un film qui ne rencontre jamais son public, c'est une parole qui reste enfermée », a-t-elle déclaré. Pour elle, le cinéma doit constituer un espace de rencontre et de dialogue entre les peuples. « Je crois profondément que l'art doit circuler, qu'il doit provoquer des rencontres, ouvrir des fenêtres, bousculer nos certitudes et nous permettre de regarder l'autre autrement », a-t-elle ajouté, invitant les Ouagalais à se mobiliser pour ce rendez-vous cinématographique. Irène Tassembédo invitant les Ouagalais à se mobiliser du 14 au 21 novembre pour prendre part à ce rendez-vous cinématographique Le coordonnateur technique du festival, Jean-Baptiste Guiard-Schmid, a indiqué que 55 films issus de 33 pays avaient été retenus pour cette édition, répartis en 34 fictions, 11 documentaires et 10 films d'animation. Cette sélection résulte du travail d'un comité international composé de 32 membres, qui a examiné 736 productions provenant de 91 pays. Les projections se dérouleront chaque soir à partir de 18 heures au siège du FESPACO. Deux séances spéciales sont prévues le vendredi 20 novembre : la première, à 18 h 30, sera consacrée au jeune public, tandis que la seconde, à 20 h 15, mettra à l'honneur la création africaine. Au-delà des projections, plusieurs activités de formation et de rencontres professionnelles figurent au programme. Un atelier de renforcement des capacités en écriture de scénarios de courts métrages est prévu du 16 au 20 novembre, ainsi qu'un concours de pitch le 21 novembre 2026. Cette édition sera également marquée par la constitution d'un jury étudiant chargé de décerner un prix spécial lors de la cérémonie de clôture. Des concerts live seront organisés chaque soir en marge des projections, et 14 films seront récompensés au terme de la compétition. Le trophée qui sera remis lors de la clôture Parmi les œuvres sélectionnées figurent notamment « Je ne suis pas fou » de Kader Ouédraogo, « Amina Traoré, l'héritage du Mandé » de Kany Dembélé, « Forêt Blanche » de Thomas Grand et Joan Bastide , « The People's Blood » de Solo Ouédraogo et « The Kankurang » de Ciesay Imran. L'entrée aux projections est libre et gratuite . Plus de 5 000 spectateurs sont attendus autour du court métrage. Sidziguin Irène Corinne SAWADOGO Minute.bf
